scenarios.title: What the user sees while the stick develops

lines.behaviour: After tapping DIPPED IT, a countdown button appears under the chat reading "75 SECONDS TO GO" and counts down.
lines.ios: The countdown takes the button slot at the bottom of the instructions chat as soon as the dip is confirmed.
lines.android: Same: the timer button becomes visible under the chat when the dip is confirmed.
lines.relation_note: FR-TIM-005 asks for two figures per timed stage: time until the next action is permitted and time until the window expires. The countdown that appears on dipping shows only the first, counting down to the moment scanning unlocks.

lines.behaviour: The count starts at 75 and reaches zero after about 70 real seconds, so each displayed second is slightly shorter than a real one.
lines.ios: 75 display units are spread over a 70-second run; the label updates roughly every 0.93 s.
lines.android: Identical arithmetic: 75 units over 70 seconds, one tick every 933 ms.
lines.relation_note: The requirement asks for the time remaining, and what is displayed is seventy-five units spread over seventy real seconds, so the figure on screen is not time: it overstates what is left for the whole of the count and would fail a check against any watch.

lines.behaviour: A coloured fill sweeps across the countdown button from left to right and reaches the far edge as the count ends.
lines.ios: A linear width animation runs for the remaining real seconds.
lines.android: A linear clip animation fills the button over the remaining real milliseconds.
lines.relation_note: The fill is a second, non-numeric rendering of the same count, so progress toward the permitted action is shown twice; it inherits the same scaled clock as the number beside it and adds nothing about expiry.

lines.behaviour: The wording switches to the singular "1 SECOND TO GO" for the last displayed second.
lines.ios: Singular title chosen when the display value is exactly 1.
lines.android: Singular resource chosen when the count is exactly 1.
lines.relation_note: Grammatical care in the countdown's wording is part of displaying remaining time legibly, which is the requirement's subject; it still serves only the next-action half of it.

lines.behaviour: When the count reaches zero the button reads "SCAN" and becomes tappable; tapping it opens the camera.
lines.ios: The button is inert while a time is shown and enabled only at zero; the tap dismisses the chat and the camera opens.
lines.android: The button is not clickable until the count finishes; the tap opens the camera screen.
lines.relation_note: The count reaching zero is what permits the next action, so the display genuinely counts to the moment FR-TIM-005 names; the button being inert until then is also the early edge of FR-TIM-011's rule that scanning is permitted only within its window, whose late edge is enforced by the expiry alert elsewhere.

lines.behaviour: Time left before the stick expires is never shown as a figure; one fixed message "...will expire in 90 seconds" appears around 90 seconds.
lines.ios: The only timing data the countdown holds is the 70/75 pair; the expiry message is a scheduled chat bubble with static text.
lines.android: Same data shape and same static bubble.
lines.relation_note: The second figure FR-TIM-005 asks for, time before the window expires, is never displayed at all. Its only trace is one fixed sentence naming ninety seconds, scheduled by elapsed time rather than read from the clock, which is a message rather than a display and is wrong whenever it appears late.

lines.behaviour: During the processing and upload waits after the scan, no time figure is shown; the waiting message carries a looping animation instead.
lines.ios: Both post-scan bubbles show a looping animation inside the bubble and no number.
lines.android: Same bubbles, same looping animation, no number.
lines.relation_note: The waits after the scan show a looping animation and no figure. If they count as active time-dependent stages, FR-TIM-005's display is absent for them; and the waiting card FR-FLW-009 asks to display the time remaining shows activity instead. They are waits on the system rather than windows on the user, so whether either requirement was meant to reach them needs a Product ruling.

lines.behaviour: The 15-minute urine-sample window has no visible timer or warning; it is checked silently when DIPPED IT is tapped.
lines.ios: The cup tap is timestamped and compared with 900 seconds at the dip tap; nothing is displayed in between.
lines.android: The cup tap is timestamped and a 15-minute window is checked at the dip tap; nothing is displayed in between.
lines.relation_note: The fifteen-minute sample window is exactly the kind of stage the requirement describes: an action is permitted only within a window. Neither the window's existence nor its remaining time is ever displayed; the first the user learns of it is when it has already been missed.

lines.behaviour: The screen stays awake during the wait, so the countdown remains visible without touching the phone.
lines.ios: The idle timer is disabled for the whole app session at start-up.
lines.android: The instructions screen keeps the screen on while it is showing.
lines.relation_note: Keeping the screen awake is what makes a glanceable countdown work, and no requirement asks for it; the timing requirements assume the display stays visible without saying how. A candidate raised with an earlier epic's review already proposes this rule, so it is recorded here without a new one.

scenarios.title: Leaving the app during the wait

lines.behaviour: Leaving the app during the countdown does not pause it; on return the count shows the correct remaining value.
lines.ios: The count is recomputed from the recorded start time whenever the app becomes active again.
lines.android: The timer view restarts from the recorded start timestamp when the screen resumes.
lines.relation_note: The displayed time stays truthful across leaving and returning because it is recomputed from the recorded start rather than resumed from where it paused, which is the arithmetic FR-TIM-003 requires after any interruption. FR-TIM-005 says nothing about interruptions; this is the behaviour its display needs anyway.

lines.behaviour: If the count finished while the app was away, the button already reads "SCAN" on return.
lines.ios: Zero remaining on resume yields the enabled title straight away.
lines.android: Zero time left on restart goes straight to the finished state.
lines.relation_note: A count that finished while the user was away is shown already finished on return, so stale remaining time is never displayed; still only the next-action half of the requirement.

lines.behaviour: No reminder, banner or system notification is raised when the count ends or the stick nears expiry while the app is in the background.
lines.ios: No local notification is ever scheduled; the in-app timer is simply invalidated on backgrounding.
lines.android: No alarm, work request or scheduled notification exists; the timer view is stopped on pause.
lines.relation_note: Both requirements exist for exactly this moment, a window nearing its end while the application is in the background, and nothing is delivered: neither platform has any path that schedules a local notification, alarm or reminder for timing, verified as an absence on both. The user finds out only by returning.

lines.behaviour: If the full 180-second window passes while the app is away, the "Time Is Up" alert appears as soon as the app returns.
lines.ios: On foregrounding, a negative remaining time reports expiry immediately and the timeout alert is shown.
lines.android: On the screen reappearing, a non-positive remaining time expires the stick immediately and the timeout alert is shown.
lines.relation_note: What the product actually does about a window lapsing in the background is tell the user on return, in the foreground, after the fact. FR-TIM-014 asks to be told before the lapse, while still away; the on-return alert is the substitute, and it reaches only users who come back.

lines.behaviour: If the app is killed mid-countdown, Android still knows when the stick was dipped; iOS forgets the dip and the countdown.
lines.ios: The clock start and the countdown start live only in memory.
lines.android: The dip time is persisted with the app state and re-evaluated when the screen next appears.
lines.relation_note: FR-STA-007, owned by the state-retention feature but squarely on point here, turns on the software recognising an incomplete test when reopened after being killed, and FR-TIM-002 requires each stage start time to be persistently retained. One platform retains the moment the stick was dipped and the other holds it only in memory, and neither uses what it has to invalidate or inform, so the substrate both requirements depend on is half present at best.

scenarios.title: Asking for notification permission, and refusing it

lines.behaviour: On the home screen the app first shows its own message "We're here to help" asking to allow notifications, with OK and No Thanks.
lines.ios: A pre-approval alert is shown from the lobby before any system prompt.
lines.android: A pre-approval alert is shown from the lobby before any system prompt.
lines.relation_note: An explanation does precede the platform prompt, as the requirement asks, but it is a generic reassurance that never says why notifications are wanted, which is the substance of that clause.

lines.behaviour: OK opens the system notification permission prompt; No Thanks dismisses without asking the system.
lines.ios: The positive button requests alert and sound authorisation from the system.
lines.android: The positive button launches the system permission request.
lines.relation_note: The requesting mechanism the first clause asks for exists and behaves properly: consent leads to the platform's own prompt, and declining is respected without troubling the system at all.

lines.behaviour: The explanation is shown once per install and skipped when the system has already granted or denied notifications.
lines.ios: Skipped when the status is authorised or denied; a stored flag prevents a second showing.
lines.android: A prompt tracker records the ask; a native should-request check also gates it.
lines.relation_note: Asking once per install and skipping the explanation once the system has an answer respects platform norms and breaches nothing in the text; whether a user who refused is ever approached again is not derivable, and the requirement is silent on it too.

lines.behaviour: Refusing notifications changes nothing in the test: no step of the guided flow checks notification permission.
lines.ios: Notification authorisation is never consulted in the chat, camera or analysis code.
lines.android: Notification permission is never consulted in the instructions, camera, analysis or chat code.
lines.relation_note: The non-blocking clause is met absolutely: no step of the guided test consults notification permission anywhere, so refusal cannot prevent a test being started, completed or reported.

lines.behaviour: The whole notification ask can be switched off remotely by a feature flag.
lines.ios: An A/B flag with default on gates the lobby prompt.
lines.android: A lobby feature flag gates the prompt.
lines.relation_note: The entire ask can be switched off remotely, so whether the software requests the permission at all is settled by configuration rather than by the software; the requirement reads as unconditional, and the production state of the switch is not derivable.

lines.behaviour: The explanation never mentions test timing; the notifications it asks for carry support and consultation messages.
lines.ios: Only push, support-chat and consultation code posts notifications.
lines.android: Only push, support-chat and consultation handlers post notifications.
lines.relation_note: The permission infrastructure exists to carry support and consultation messages, not timing. The corpus ties this permission to the timing notification's needs, and an explanation written for a different purpose cannot explain the purpose the corpus wants the permission for; it is also further evidence that no timing notification exists to be permitted.

scenarios.title: Edges of the countdown

lines.behaviour: Tapping SCAN late, even after the 90-second warning, still opens the camera; only the 180-second expiry blocks the test.
lines.ios: The scan tap dismisses the chat unconditionally; blocking comes only from the clock expiring.
lines.android: The scan trigger opens the camera unconditionally; blocking comes only from the scheduled expiry.
lines.relation_note: FR-TIM-011 permits scanning only within the validated window and invalidates after it. Seen from this feature, the window's end is the only gate there is: the ninety-second warning does not block, and a late tap short of three minutes still opens the camera, which matches the requirement's shape. The enforcement itself belongs to the scanning-window feature.

lines.behaviour: The chat says "wait 75 seconds" and the button counts 75, but the button unlocks after 70 real seconds.
lines.ios: Copy and display agree on 75; the underlying run time is 70.
lines.android: Copy and display agree on 75; the underlying run time is 75 minus a 5-second offset.
lines.relation_note: The copy promises seventy-five seconds, the display counts seventy-five, and seventy real seconds govern, so the one place remaining time is displayed it is displayed wrong; flagged by the extraction as behaviour not to copy.

lines.behaviour: How long after dipping the user tapped SCAN is recorded in analytics, not shown to the user.
lines.ios: The scan tap event carries elapsed seconds derived from the 180-second clock.
lines.android: A scan-timer event carries elapsed seconds since the dip timestamp.
lines.relation_note: The time between dipping and scanning is measured and reported for analytics but never shown or kept with the test. It is the very quantity the timing windows exist to bound, and the corpus is silent about a measurement the product already makes.

scenarios.title: Stick timer lapses: "Time Is Up", then the troubleshooting chat explains and routes

lines.behaviour: Three minutes after the dip tap, if no scan has completed, a full-screen alert titled "Time Is Up" interrupts whatever the user is doing.
lines.ios: A single 180-second clock starts on the dip tap; when it ends the alert is presented over the instructions or camera screen.
lines.android: The dip time is stored and a 180-second deadline is scheduled; when it passes the same alert is shown over the instructions or camera screen.
lines.relation_note: The user is informed promptly that the test is over, wherever they are in the flow, which is the requirement's premise; but the alert names neither the reason nor what to do next, which are the two things the requirement actually asks for at this moment.

lines.behaviour: The alert body reads "You can no longer use the stick for this test." It states the consequence, not why.
lines.ios: Title "Time Is Up", body as quoted; the target's own alert table has no entry for this alert so the shared wording is used.
lines.android: Title "Time Is Up", body as quoted, error-styled dialog with no icon.
lines.relation_note: Consequence without reason: the body says the stick can no longer be used, not why. The reason the requirement wants in the invalidation message arrives only on the following screen.

lines.behaviour: The alert offers one button, "Continue" on iOS and "CONTINUE" on Android; it cannot be dismissed any other way.
lines.ios: One title-case button; no secondary button, no close control, and tapping the dimmed backdrop does nothing.
lines.android: One upper-case button; the dialog is not cancelable, so the back button and outside taps do nothing.
lines.relation_note: The extraction left this line unmapped, but the dismissal mechanics serve the informing duty: the single undismissable button is the only exit and it leads to the screen that states the reason, so the reason is guaranteed to be presented eventually. The platforms differ only in the button's casing.

lines.behaviour: Tapping the button opens a chat headed "STICK NO LONGER VALID" that finally states the reason: more than 3 minutes since dipping.
lines.ios: The alert's button stops the clock and replaces the current screen with the troubleshooting chat for the timeout flow.
lines.android: The alert's button clears the in-memory timed-out marker and opens the troubleshooting screen for the timeout flow.
lines.relation_note: The reason is delivered in full, more than three minutes since dipping, but one screen after the invalidation message rather than in it, which is where the requirement places it.

lines.behaviour: The chat then asks "did you extract the stick from its wrapping?" with "YES, I EXTRACTED THE STICK" and "NO, I DID NOT EXTRACT IT".
lines.ios: Two-option button in the timeout chat; yes adds the 'order new kit' branch, no adds the 'kit is valid' branch.
lines.android: Identical two-option button and branching in the flavour's troubleshooting script.
lines.relation_note: The extraction read this as outside the requirement, but the triage question decides when the requirement's own instruction applies: only the answer that the stick was extracted leads to the new-kit branch. The requirement presumes every timing invalidation consumes the kit; the product first asks whether it actually did.

lines.behaviour: Answering yes shows "ORDER NEW KIT": the kit is single-use and cannot be reused; the only button is "TO CUSTOMER SUPPORT".
lines.ios: The 'the extracted-kit timeout' branch: two bubbles then a single support button that leaves the chat for the support screen.
lines.android: Same branch and button; support opens the support screen.
lines.relation_note: The spent-kit branch tells the user the kit is single-use and cannot be reused, and routes to support, which also delivers FR-SUP-003's promise for a condition the user cannot resolve; but it never instructs them to repeat the test, so the requirement's instruction clause is half-delivered at best.

lines.behaviour: Answering no shows "KIT IS VALID", reassures the kit is still usable, and "BACK TO HOME VIEW" returns home with no failure recorded.
lines.ios: The order is marked a dry run locally; the recent-failure warning on the home screen is skipped when the status is dry run.
lines.android: The order is marked a dry run and the recent-test alert is flagged as already viewed, so the home screen does not warn.
lines.relation_note: The requirement instructs a new kit on every timing invalidation; here the product deliberately tells the user the opposite, that the unopened kit is still valid, and records no failure. The branch is sensible and truthful, and a literal reading of the requirement would forbid it, which is a tension for Product to resolve rather than a defect.

lines.behaviour: Unless the server has switched this variant to single-kit mode, the yes/no answer is kept only on the device and the server is not told.
lines.ios: The 'stick was used' trigger only updates the server when single-kit is on; the build default is off and only server settings can change it.
lines.android: Same: the 'stick was used' trigger updates the server only when single-kit is on; build default off, server init may override.

lines.behaviour: Its body says the sample must be tested within 15 minutes, this kit can no longer be used, and a new one will be sent.
lines.ios: Title "Urine sample expired" with a clock icon; body as quoted.
lines.android: Title "Urine sample expired", no icon; body as quoted.
lines.relation_note: The fullest invalidation message in the product: the rule, the consequence, and the kit's replacement all in one alert. It is still phrased as an offer to send a new kit rather than an instruction to repeat the test with one, which is the closest the product comes to the requirement's second clause.

lines.behaviour: The only button is "Support" ("SUPPORT" on Android); there is no troubleshooting chat and no way to continue or go home directly.
lines.ios: Positive tap ends the instructions with 'support requested'; support is shown and afterwards the flow finishes to home.
lines.android: Primary tap clears the in-memory marker and opens support with return-to-home on finish.
lines.relation_note: A support-only exit fits FR-SUP-003, since an expired sample is nothing the user can fix; the requirement under map does not prescribe the exit, and the alert's single route means the user cannot decline the conversation and simply go home.

lines.behaviour: After a sample expiry, only Android warns "This kit has been used" on the next attempt; iOS starts the new test without comment.
lines.ios: The support-only exit never records a failed test, so the home screen's recent-failure warning does not fire.
lines.android: The expired-sample status is processed as a failed order, so the recent-failure warning appears for the next 24 hours.
lines.relation_note: FR-KIT-007's twenty-four-hour gate exists to catch the next attempt after an invalidated test, and after a sample expiry it fires on one platform and not on the other, because only one records the failure. The same timing failure thus produces different warnings on the next attempt depending on the phone in hand.

lines.behaviour: Nothing warns the user that the 15-minute sample window is running or about to lapse before they tap dip.
lines.ios: No countdown or bubble between the urine step and the dip step; the check happens silently at the dip tap.
lines.android: Same: no countdown or bubble for the sample window; the check happens at the dip tap.
lines.relation_note: The sample window is an active time-dependent stage whose remaining time FR-TIM-005 requires to be displayed, and nothing displays it or even reveals it exists; the first the user hears of the window is its failure. The requirement is owned by the timing-display feature; this line is the invalidation-side view of the same absence.

scenarios.title: Timer lapses while scanning, during analysis, or before a retry scan

lines.behaviour: If the 3 minutes lapse while scanning, the camera stops and "Time Is Up" appears over it, leading to the same chat.
lines.ios: The camera stops taking frames and shows its error stage; the coordinator's timer handler presents the alert while the scan is still unfinished.
lines.android: The next processed frame sees the deadline passed, stops the preview, marks the timeout and the camera screen shows the alert.
lines.relation_note: The window lapsing mid-scan stops the capture and informs the user, which is FR-TIM-011's invalidation enforced inside the camera; the message is the same reason-less alert, so FR-TIM-012's gaps repeat here unchanged.

lines.behaviour: Once a scan has succeeded and analysis begins, a lapsing timer produces no message at all; the analysis simply continues.
lines.ios: The timeout alert is disarmed the moment the camera is about to hand over to analysis; the clock keeps running until the local analysis succeeds.
lines.android: Analysis re-schedules the deadline and, if it passes, marks the order timed out, but the analysis screen has no alert for it.
lines.relation_note: FR-TIM-011's invalidation clause reads as unconditional, yet once a capture has succeeded the lapsing window is ignored and the result is delivered. Whether a window that expires after a successful capture invalidates is a boundary the requirement does not state, and the product answers it silently.

lines.behaviour: If analysis rejects the scan and returns the user to the camera after the window lapsed, "Time Is Up" appears immediately on re-entry.
lines.ios: Re-entering the camera after a boundary error re-arms the alert; on appear, a negative remaining time shows the timeout error at once.
lines.android: On camera appear with the timed-out flag set, the preview is hidden and the timeout is processed, showing the alert.
lines.relation_note: The retry path honours the expired window: re-entering the camera after a rejected attempt is blocked at once when the window has lapsed, which enforces FR-TIM-011, and the user learns only then that the retry window had already closed; the alert again gives no reason.

lines.behaviour: When time runs out in the camera, whatever was captured is uploaded silently as a timed-out attempt; the user is not told.
lines.ios: This target always uploads the timed-out exam (with a trace); the upload runs in the background with no message.
lines.android: The build flag for uploading timed-out exams is on; the runner's timeout handler uploads in the background with no message.
lines.relation_note: Nothing in the corpus says whether a timed-out attempt's captured data is kept, transmitted or discarded; the product transmits it in the background without telling the user, which Product should adopt or reject deliberately rather than inherit.

lines.behaviour: When time runs out on the instructions screen before scanning, nothing is uploaded; only the timeout status is kept on the device.
lines.ios: The coordinator marks the order timed out locally and shows the alert; no exam exists to upload and the server is not called.
lines.android: The timeout is recorded in the stored state and order; no upload path runs from the instructions screen.
lines.relation_note: A timeout before any scan leaves only a local record and the backend is never told; no requirement addresses reporting invalidations, which is why a candidate below asks for it.

scenarios.title: Server declares the stick dry after upload

lines.behaviour: When the server reports the stick was not properly dipped, "Test Results Problem" replaces results: "Your stick and kit are no longer valid for use."
lines.ios: After upload, a 'dry stick' status from the server raises the dry-stick alert in the analysis chat.
lines.android: After upload, a 'a dry stick' error from the server maps to the dry-stick error state and the analysis screen shows the alert.
lines.relation_note: If a stick the server declares dry is a timing failure, this is an invalidation on timing grounds delivered with a generic title and a body that states only invalidity: neither the reason nor any next step is in the message, the same displacement as the stick timeout.

lines.behaviour: That alert gives neither a reason nor a next step; the explanation about patches not dipped comes only in the chat after the button.
lines.ios: Single button "Continue"; tapping it opens the dry-stick troubleshooting chat.
lines.android: Single button "CONTINUE"; tapping it opens the dry-stick troubleshooting screen.
lines.relation_note: The reason, patches not properly dipped, is again delivered one screen after the invalidation message, behind the alert's single button.

lines.behaviour: The dry-stick chat says the kit and stick are no longer valid and offers only "TO CUSTOMER SUPPORT"; there is no way to retest.
lines.ios: After the continue button the 'order new kit' bubbles are added, ending in a single support button.
lines.android: Same continuation and support button.
lines.relation_note: The user is told the kit and stick are no longer valid and routed to support, which fits FR-SUP-003 for a condition they cannot resolve; the requirement's instruction to repeat the test with a new kit is absent, as everywhere.

lines.behaviour: Whether a dry stick counts as a timing failure is decided by the server; the app only relays the verdict.
lines.ios: The app maps a server status string to the alert; no local timing check produces it.
lines.android: The app maps a server error string to the alert; no local timing check produces it.
lines.relation_note: The requirement turns on the words 'invalidated on timing grounds', and for this invalidation the grounds live at the server: the application only relays a verdict it cannot explain. Whether a dry stick counts as timing, and whether the app can ever state its reason, needs a Product ruling.

scenarios.title: Backgrounded, idle, or relaunched while a timing window is running

lines.behaviour: Backgrounding during the 3-minute window does not pause the clock; if it lapsed while away, "Time Is Up" shows as soon as the app returns.
lines.ios: The clock is wall-clock based; on entering background the timer is cancelled and on foreground it is re-armed for the remainder or fired at once.
lines.android: The deadline is recomputed from the stored dip time on every resume; if already passed, the stick-expired handling runs immediately.
lines.relation_note: The invalidation message survives an interruption: the window keeps running against the recorded start and the alert is presented the moment the user returns, with the same content gaps it has in the foreground.

lines.behaviour: No notification, sound or badge is sent while the app is in the background; the user learns of the timeout only by returning.
lines.ios: Nothing schedules a local notification for the timer; the alert is presented only in the foreground.
lines.android: Nothing schedules an alarm, job or notification for the deadline; the scheduled callback is cancelled on pause.
lines.relation_note: The moment FR-TIM-014 exists for, the window ending while the user is away, passes in silence: no notification, sound or badge on either platform, verified as an absence. The foreground alert on return is the only delivery vehicle the product has. The requirement is owned by the timing-display feature; this is the invalidation-side view of the same absence.

lines.behaviour: The usual 15-minute idle restart is suspended while the stick clock runs, so a long absence still ends in the timeout message, not a restart.
lines.ios: The foreground reset is skipped while the shared clock has a start time ('critical path'); the idle limit is otherwise 15 minutes.
lines.android: The idle reset is skipped while the scan timer is running or has already timed out; the idle limit is otherwise 15 minutes.
lines.relation_note: FR-STA-003 forbids an inactivity timeout while a test is active, and this is that clause holding under pressure: the idle restart that applies everywhere else is suspended while the stick window runs, which is exactly what lets the invalidation message be delivered after a long absence instead of the flow being silently discarded.

lines.behaviour: Returning to the troubleshooting chat after 15+ minutes away restarts the app on iOS but leaves the chat in place on Android.
lines.ios: The clock is stopped when the alert is acknowledged, so the idle-restart rule applies again during the chat.
lines.android: The timed-out flag stays set until the home screen clears it, so the idle restart stays suspended during the chat.
lines.relation_note: Once the test is invalidated no requirement protects the explanation screen itself, and the platforms disagree: a long absence on that screen restarts one platform and leaves the other in place, so whether the reason survives the user's absence is currently chance.
lines.pm_comment: depends if it is after the cup is full or not

lines.behaviour: If the app is fully relaunched during the window, no timing message ever appears; the test starts over from home with the same kit.
lines.ios: The clock lives only in memory and is gone after a relaunch; nothing remembers the dip.
lines.android: The dip time is stored, but the home screen clears it on arrival, so nothing remembers it either.
lines.relation_note: A relaunch during the window is the case FR-STA-007 describes, reopening after termination during an active test, and none of its three obligations is delivered: nothing identifies the lapsed test, nothing invalidates it, and no message ever appears, so the same kit is treated as fresh. FR-TIM-002's persistently retained start time exists on one platform only and is discarded on arrival home, which is why nothing can be said. Both requirements are owned elsewhere; this line is where their absence becomes a reusable dipped stick.

scenarios.title: Window lengths, the advance warning, and the next attempt

lines.behaviour: The stick window is 3 minutes from the dip tap; the on-screen countdown covers only 75 seconds, after which the button reads "SCAN".
lines.ios: Timer button data: 70 seconds of actual run shown against a 75-second display; total test time 180 seconds.
lines.android: Timer button data: 75 minus 5 offset against a 75-second display; total test time 180 seconds.
lines.relation_note: The displayed count covers only the first seventy-five units of a three-minute window, so most of the invalidation window runs with no display at all; FR-TIM-005's expiry half, owned by the timing-display feature, is the missing piece this boundary exposes.

lines.behaviour: Before time runs out the chat warns "Click Scan now. The stick will expire in 90 seconds." — the only advance warning of invalidation.
lines.ios: Last real-time bubble of the scanning group, shown after the countdown finishes.
lines.android: Same bubble in the flavour's instructions script.
lines.relation_note: The only advance warning of invalidation anywhere is one scheduled sentence in the foreground chat. It is the nearest thing the product has to the expiry display FR-TIM-005 wants and to the about-to-expire warning FR-TIM-014 wants, and it is neither: fixed text rather than a reading of the clock, and foreground only.

lines.behaviour: Within 24 hours of a timeout where the stick was extracted, starting again shows "This kit has been used" with support and new-kit buttons.
lines.ios: Buttons "Support" / "I Have A New Kit"; the check uses the last failed-test time and the 24-hour minimum between tests.
lines.android: Buttons "SUPPORT" / "I HAVE A NEW KIT"; the check uses the failed-order timestamp and a 24-hour block window.
lines.relation_note: The gate FR-KIT-007 requires exists and fires within twenty-four hours of a timeout where the stick was extracted, with a message and a confirmation of holding a new kit. It is also where the new-kit statement FR-TIM-012 wanted at invalidation is actually delivered, one attempt later than the requirement places it.

lines.behaviour: Choosing the new-kit option opens a "New Test" page: "A new kit is required" — the clearest statement anywhere that retesting needs a new kit.
lines.ios: A full-screen page with sections "A new kit is required" and "Customer Support" and an OK button back to home.
lines.android: The same page, launched from the alert's secondary button, with OK returning home.
lines.relation_note: The plainest statement in the product that a new kit is required exists on a dedicated page, reached from the used-kit warning on the next attempt; FR-TIM-012's instruction is therefore in the product but two taps and one attempt away from the moment the requirement names.

lines.behaviour: That warning asks rather than blocks: after acknowledging it the test proceeds and nothing checks that a new kit is actually used.
lines.ios: Choosing the new-kit option marks the warning as presented; the next start passes the check.
lines.android: Choosing the new-kit option marks the recent-test alert as viewed; the next start passes the check.
lines.relation_note: Confirmation without verification is what FR-KIT-007's text asks, and the corpus accepts that because FR-KIT-004 is meant to catch actual reuse at the scan; but that catch depends on the backend knowing the kit was consumed, which a timeout before any scan never tells it, so for these kits the confirmation is the only control there is.

lines.behaviour: If the user said they never extracted the stick, the next attempt shows no warning and the same kit is treated as fresh.
lines.ios: The recent-failure check is skipped when the order status is dry run.
lines.android: A dry-run status marks the recent-test alert as already viewed.
lines.relation_note: Read literally, FR-KIT-007's gate should fire after any invalidated test within the window; the product exempts the case where the user said the stick was never extracted and treats the kit as fresh, a deliberate exception the corpus does not have and should either adopt or overrule.

lines.behaviour: All timing windows run on the device clock; changing the phone's time changes when a test is invalidated.
lines.ios: Start and remaining time come from the current date; nothing uses a monotonic clock or server time.
lines.android: Deadlines are computed from the current system time in milliseconds against stored timestamps.
lines.relation_note: FR-TIM-004 requires a time source the user cannot move, and every window here runs on the device clock, so changing the phone's time changes when a test is invalidated. The requirement is owned by the timers feature; this is the invalidation consequence of not having it.

lines.behaviour: The 15-minute urine window and 3-minute stick window are fixed in the build on both platforms; neither is adjustable from the server.
lines.ios: Both values are compile-time configuration of the target; the sample window is a literal 900 seconds.
lines.android: Both values are compile-time build fields or constants of the flavour.
lines.relation_note: Both window lengths are fixed in the application and cannot be changed at run time, which is exactly what FR-TIM-001 requires of timing values; the cost the requirement accepts, that tuning a window means a release, is visible here.

scenarios.title: The message sequence beside the countdown

lines.behaviour: Right after DIPPED IT, the user's own line "The stick was dipped and placed on the Color-Board." and a SCANNING header appear above the countdown.
lines.ios: User bubble and section header are the first real-time items of the scanning group.
lines.android: Same two items open the scanning group.
lines.relation_note: The wait's content is opened by the flow itself: the echoed confirmation and a section header appear unbidden the moment the timed wait begins, which is the required shape, presented by the flow rather than fetched by the user. No time is shown yet.

lines.behaviour: Over the next 70 seconds, eight messages arrive one at a time, each after a typing indicator, at intervals fixed in the app.
lines.ios: Each bubble names a bundled timing key; the engine waits that interval before showing it.
lines.android: Each bubble names a bundled timing resource; the resolver uses it as an override interval.
lines.relation_note: Content that changes as the period elapses is delivered as messages appended one at a time at intervals fixed in the application, meeting the changing-content and fixed-thresholds clauses; nothing in the sequence displays the time remaining, which is the clause the same sentence of the requirement leads with.

lines.behaviour: The messages move from reassurance and an explanation of the wait, through scanning tips, to "We're ready. Let's scan." as the count ends.
lines.ios: "We're ready" lands about 69 seconds after the header, just before the button unlocks.
lines.android: "We're ready" lands about 69 seconds after the header, just before the button unlocks.
lines.relation_note: The content is a genuine function of elapsed time, moving from reassurance through preparation to readiness just as the wait ends, which is exactly the mechanism the requirement describes; the remaining-time display is absent throughout.

lines.behaviour: The fifth message is a short video showing how to scan, with a "replay" control the user may ignore.
lines.ios: A replayable video bubble with a replay button; replays are counted in analytics.
lines.android: Same bubble type, same replay button and analytics.
lines.relation_note: Instructional content placed inside the wait, with a replay the user may ignore: the card is used to teach, which the requirement permits since its content belongs to the approved content set, and ignoring the video costs nothing.

lines.behaviour: About 20 seconds after "We're ready", a last message "Click Scan now. The stick will expire in 90 seconds." appears if unscanned.
lines.ios: Scheduled 19 s typing plus 1 s after the ready message; only shown while the chat is still open.
lines.android: Same schedule; only shown while the chat is still open.
lines.relation_note: The only content that ever states remaining time, and it is a fixed sentence scheduled by elapsed time rather than a display read from a clock, so it is correct only when nothing has delayed it.

lines.behaviour: None of the messages needs a tap; only the SCAN button moves the flow on, so ignoring the messages changes nothing.
lines.ios: The scanning group has no button items other than the timer button and the optional replay.
lines.android: Same group content; the chat advances on schedule without input.
lines.relation_note: The optionality clause in full: no message requires a tap and nothing in the sequence gates progress, so not reading the content affects neither the conduct nor the validity of the test.

lines.behaviour: Tapping SCAN the moment it unlocks leaves the chat at once, even though later messages have not appeared.
lines.ios: The scan tap dismisses the whole chat; pending bubbles are abandoned.
lines.android: The scan trigger opens the camera; pending bubbles are abandoned.
lines.relation_note: The yielding clause: the moment the flow lets the user act, acting wins, and the unshown remainder of the content is abandoned without penalty.

lines.behaviour: Each message arrives with its own sound; iOS turns sound on when the instructions open, Android keeps the user's last mute choice.
lines.ios: Sound is forced on when entering the instructions chat regardless of the previous setting.
lines.android: The chat is created with the user's saved sound preference.
lines.relation_note: The wait's messages are voiced, so the card is part of the spoken flow FR-FLW-008 governs, and that requirement says a silenced flow stays silent for the remainder of the test. One platform overrides the user's earlier silencing when this stage opens and the other honours it, so the clause holds on one platform only.

lines.behaviour: Arrival of the ready and expiry messages, and video replays, are reported to analytics.
lines.ios: Show events "Ready To Scan Bubble Appeared" and "Scan now alert"; replay event "Replay Video Click".
lines.android: Same three events declared in the script.
lines.relation_note: Whether the ready and expiry messages were reached, and whether the video was replayed, is already measured by the product; no requirement addresses instrumentation of the wait.

scenarios.title: The waiting bubble after the scan

lines.behaviour: After the scan a PROCESSING header and "Hold on while we analyze your scanned images." appear with a looping animation inside the bubble.
lines.ios: The bubble carries a named progress animation with intro, loop and outro segments.
lines.android: The bubble carries the same named animation, played as intro then infinite loop.
lines.relation_note: The post-scan wait gets a card presented by the flow, which is the required shape, but it displays no time and its content does not change as the period elapses; it shows activity instead.

lines.behaviour: When the phone finishes analysing, "Done 🙂" appears and the animation plays out to its finished state.
lines.ios: Adding the next bubble ends the outstanding animation with its outro.
lines.android: Adding the next bubble flags the previous one and its animation plays the outro.
lines.relation_note: The content changes once, on the event of finishing rather than as a function of elapsed time; telling the user the wait has ended is useful, but it is not the mechanism the requirement describes, and no figure is ever shown.

lines.behaviour: Then an ANALYZING header and "Fantastic. Please wait while we analyze your test results." appear with a looping animation during upload.
lines.ios: Bubble with a progress animation and a 45-second threshold.
lines.android: Same bubble, same threshold.
lines.relation_note: The upload wait repeats the same pattern: one message, a looping animation, no time, no time-driven change of content.

lines.behaviour: The waiting message's text never changes; only the animation loops, and no time figure is shown.
lines.ios: The bubble has one text key; the loop segment repeats until the next item arrives.
lines.android: The bubble has one text key; the loop segment repeats infinitely until the next item arrives.
lines.relation_note: The longest wait in the flow never changes its content over time at all. Whether that breaches the requirement turns on its opening words: this wait is indeterminate rather than timed, so a Product ruling is needed on whether the card rule was meant to reach waits of unknown length.

lines.behaviour: If the upload wait exceeds 45 seconds, an alert "Connectivity Issue" interrupts with a message about checking the internet connection and OK.
lines.ios: The threshold trigger shows the first connectivity alert when the exam is still uploading.
lines.android: The threshold trigger sets a sending-info error shown as the first connectivity alert.
lines.relation_note: A fixed interval guards the upload wait and interrupts it with a connectivity alert; no requirement asks for a stalled wait to be noticed at all, so the guard, its threshold and its wording are all unspecified.

lines.behaviour: Tapping OK restarts the 45-second wait with the same message; a second timeout offers "Retry" or "Support".
lines.ios: Dismissal publishes a retry event that restarts the threshold; more than one report escalates to the Retry/Support alert.
lines.android: Dismissal fires a retry event that reschedules the threshold; a second timeout escalates to the Retry/Support alert.
lines.relation_note: A second timeout offers support alongside retry, which is FR-SUP-003's shape: the software cannot move forward and hands the user a way out. Whether one failed interval already counts as a condition the user cannot resolve themselves is a judgement the corpus does not make.

lines.behaviour: If the phone has no internet at the 45-second mark, "No Internet Connection" is shown instead, and OK returns to the wait.
lines.ios: Reachability is checked first; unreachable shows the no-network alert without counting a report.
lines.android: Connectivity is checked first; disconnected shows the no-network alert.
lines.relation_note: The guard distinguishes an absent connection from a transfer that is failing and words the alert accordingly; nothing in the corpus asks the software to tell those cases apart.

lines.behaviour: Choosing Support leaves the analysis wait and opens support.
lines.ios: Support dismisses the analysis as cancelled with support requested.
lines.android: Support opens the support screen from the alert.
lines.relation_note: Choosing support abandons the wait and reaches the support channel, which delivers FR-SUP-003's promise for this blocked state; the cost, that getting help ends the analysis wait, is not something the requirement weighs.

lines.behaviour: On Android only, a second timeout while the result is already queued for the clinician skips the alert and proceeds to results.
lines.ios: No such branch; the second timeout always shows Retry/Support unless the upload has already finished.
lines.android: If a connectivity alert was already shown and partner transmission is pending, the flow continues to results.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: While a time-dependent stage of the test flow is active, the software shall prevent the device display from turning off.
candidate_new_requirements.why: The countdown, the timed instructions and the expiry warning all live on the screen; if the display sleeps mid-wait the user loses every timing cue the corpus requires them to have, and on most devices the display would sleep well inside the three-minute window. ACR keeps the screen awake throughout the test on both platforms, and no corpus requirement mentions display sleep at all — the display requirements presume a screen that stays visible without saying so.
candidate_new_requirements.note: Could join the timing-display feature's requirements rather than stand alone; scoping it to time-dependent stages rather than the whole session is deliberate, since ACR's whole-session approach is broader than the need.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: When a test is invalidated on timing grounds, the software shall record the invalidation and its reason against the test, and shall treat the kit as no longer usable for testing.
candidate_new_requirements.why: FR-TIM-006 stops at preventing and explaining, and FR-TIM-012 at informing and instructing; nothing requires the failed attempt to be written down or the kit spent. Yet FR-KIT-007's outcome-matched message on the next attempt, and any replacement-kit remedy promised to the user, both depend on that record existing. ACR records it deliberately on both platforms.
candidate_new_requirements.note: Prefer amending FR-TIM-012, which already governs what happens at the moment of a timing invalidation, rather than adding a new requirement.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: Following a timing invalidation, the software shall establish whether the reagent stick was exposed, and where the user confirms it was not, shall record the attempt as a test not performed and may permit the same kit to be used for a later test.
candidate_new_requirements.why: FR-TIM-009 stops at invalidate-and-prevent, but the deadline can pass before the stick was ever exposed, and in that case nothing was actually spent. ACR resolves this with a recovery conversation whose second branch un-spends the kit on the user's word alone. Either that recovery is wanted — in which case it must be required, together with an explicit acceptance that the only verification is self-report — or it is not, in which case the current behaviour must be forbidden. The corpus currently does neither.
candidate_new_requirements.note: Prefer amending FR-TIM-009, or folding into FR-TIM-012's recovery wording; the self-report-only verification is a Product decision that must be made in the open.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: In demonstration mode the software shall apply none of the timing limits of this section, neither minimum durations nor permitted completion windows.
candidate_new_requirements.why: FR-TIM-008 lifts only the minimum times in demonstration mode, and FR-TIM-011 says nothing about demonstration at all; ACR's two platforms resolved that silence in opposite directions, one applying no deadline in demo and the other a shortened one. Whichever answer Product wants, the corpus currently permits both at once.
candidate_new_requirements.note: Prefer widening FR-TIM-008's demonstration-mode sentence to cover the whole timing section rather than adding a requirement.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: The software shall record, with each captured image, the elapsed time since the start of the timed stage during which it was captured.
candidate_new_requirements.why: The validated scanning window is enforced at capture but evidenced nowhere in the record the corpus asks for: the per-image record requirement covers camera parameters only, and nothing preserves proof that a given image fell inside the window. ACR stamps every image deliberately, and any downstream review of window compliance rests on that stamp.
candidate_new_requirements.note: Could be an amendment to the existing per-image record requirement in the camera area rather than a new TIM requirement.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: Where a test is invalidated on timing grounds after image capture has begun, the software shall transmit the captured images and their timing record to the backend for quality review, and the retention of that material shall be disclosed to the user.
candidate_new_requirements.why: ACR uploads timed-out attempts, images and processing record included, on both platforms and never tells the user; the corpus neither requires nor forbids this, and data leaving the device from a test the user believes dead is a behaviour that must be either mandated or prohibited, not left unstated. The existing retention requirement only bounds data around a transmission it assumes was intended.
candidate_new_requirements.note: Needs a Product decision on whether failed-attempt data may leave the device at all; the disclosure half may belong with the consent documents rather than the timing section. Touches the E04 candidate on discarding data of invalidated tests.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: The software shall record the actual elapsed time of each timed stage of the test, and shall include those times in the data transmitted with the test.
candidate_new_requirements.why: The timing windows exist because elapsed time bears on the validity of the result, and the shipping product already measures the interval between dipping and scanning, but reports it only to analytics; nothing requires the measured times to accompany the test record itself, where a clinician-facing system could use them.
candidate_new_requirements.note: If the transmitted payload is specified under the data-transmission requirements, prefer adding it there rather than as a new TIM rule.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: When a test is invalidated on timing grounds, the software shall state in the invalidation message itself which timing rule was not met, and shall instruct the user to repeat the test with a new kit where the kit has been consumed. Where the software establishes that the kit was not consumed, it shall state instead that the kit remains usable.
candidate_new_requirements.why: The shipping product spreads the reason and the consequence over as many as three screens, never says to repeat the test, and has a branch the current requirement forbids by silence: a user who never opened the kit is truthfully told it is still usable. As written, FR-TIM-012 cannot be satisfied while keeping that sensible branch, so the departure should be decided rather than inherited.
candidate_new_requirements.note: An amendment to FR-TIM-012 rather than a new requirement.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: When a test is invalidated and the kit has been consumed, the software shall report the invalidation to the backend when connectivity permits, so that the consumed kit can be recognised if it is presented again.
candidate_new_requirements.why: A kit spent by a timeout before any scan is unknown to the backend: the consumed-kit answer stays on the device, nothing is transmitted, and the confirmation gate on the next attempt asks rather than checks. The reuse detection the corpus relies on can therefore never fire for exactly the kits most likely to be presented again, and a relaunch during the window erases even the local record.
candidate_new_requirements.note: An earlier epic's review proposed reporting the invalidation of tests ended by termination; cleaner as one rule covering every invalidation than as two.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: The scanning-time window shall apply to the capture of the Test Board: a capture completed within the window shall remain valid although the window expires while analysis is in progress, and the software shall not invalidate the test on that ground.
candidate_new_requirements.why: FR-TIM-011's invalidation clause reads as unconditional, but the shipping product lets the window lapse silently once a capture has succeeded and delivers the result. Either that is right and the requirement needs its boundary stated, or every analysis that outlives the window must be discarded, which is a different product; the choice should be made deliberately.
candidate_new_requirements.note: Prefer amending FR-TIM-011, which the scanning-window feature owns; raised here because the silence is what the user experiences.

candidate_new_requirements.statement: Where the software is waiting on processing or transmission and the wait exceeds a defined interval, the software shall inform the user, shall distinguish an absent connection from a transfer that is failing, and shall offer a route to support where the condition persists after retry.
candidate_new_requirements.why: The longest wait in the flow is actively guarded in the shipping product: a fixed interval raises an alert, repetition escalates to retry or support, and a missing connection is named as such. The corpus describes only a passive waiting card, so a specification written from it alone would ship an unguarded indefinite wait with no exit.
candidate_new_requirements.note: Sits between the flow and transmission areas; if the transmission requirements gain a stalled-transfer rule, fold this into it rather than keeping two.

FR-TIM-001.reasoning: Every element the requirement names exists for the stick stage: a defined start event (the user's confirmation tap), a minimum duration enforced at capture, a permitted completion window, and an expiry behaviour that blocks and explains — all fixed in the build with no runtime path to change them. Three things keep it from full. The platforms disagree where the completion window ends, at capture or at result, so one of the four elements has two definitions. The displayed minimum and the enforced minimum deliberately differ by five seconds, so the defined value and the presented value are not the same number. And a latent, unconfirmed defect on one platform may let the expiry cutoff silently lapse for a subsequent test in the same session, which undermines the definedness of the expiry behaviour itself.

FR-TIM-002.reasoning: Recording happens: both platforms stamp the start at the defined start event and every window is derived from that stamp. Persistent retention does not survive contact with reality: one platform holds the start only in memory and loses it to any process death, and the other writes it to durable storage but wipes it the moment the home screen next appears, so no relaunch on either platform ever finds a retained start to resume or enforce against. The requirement's words are met for as long as the process lives, which is precisely when persistence is not needed.

FR-TIM-003.reasoning: One rule covers every interruption the requirement names and more: elapsed time is always recomputed from the retained start instant, never resumed from a paused counter. Backgrounding, screen lock and calls cost nothing; an expiry that fell due during an absence fires immediately on return; a countdown whose end passed while away appears already finished; and rescans run under the original clock. Two caveats within the text's bounds: the rule holds only within a process lifetime, the loss beyond that belonging to FR-TIM-002; and enforcement is passive — nothing fires while the app is closed — which the requirement does not forbid.

FR-TIM-004.reasoning: Every clock in the timed flow reads the device's wall clock, so the user can extend any window by setting the clock back or trigger expiry by setting it forward — the exact defeat the requirement exists to prevent, and it applies to every window in this epic including the sample limit. The single immunity, to time-zone changes, comes free from comparing absolute instants rather than from any protective design. The requirement's own notes record it as future development at the lowest priority; ACR is the unprotected state those notes describe.

FR-TIM-006.reasoning: The requirement's whole shape is present: elapsed time is measured from the sample-collection confirmation to the next confirmation, timed silently with no countdown, checked at the moment the user tries to proceed, and an over-limit attempt is met with a blocking explanatory alert and no way onward with that kit. Four gaps keep it from full. The check ships in only one regional build, where the requirement is unconditional. The measurement start survives process death on one platform only, so the check can silently vanish mid-test. The two platforms disagree whether a sample at exactly the limit passes or fails, so the defined limit is not one definition. And the whole window rides the user-adjustable device clock, which is FR-TIM-004's unimplemented business. ACR also enforces 15 minutes where the corpus currently notes 30 — a value the timing study owns, not a defect.

FR-TIM-007.reasoning: The sequencing half is solid: nothing actionable exists until the dip is confirmed, and every preceding instruction must be completed through its own control first. The timing half is met in effect but not to the letter. The actionable moment arrives five seconds before the stated residence time, a deliberate head start whose difference the scanner later absorbs by withholding capture; the control is visible from the first second of the wait, locked and counting, rather than presented only after the time has elapsed; and the spoken 'ready' instruction rides a separate scripted timeline that coincides with the unlock rather than being driven by it. Whether a locked, counting control counts as withholding the instruction is a reading Product must make; ACR's own answer is that the instruction is the unlock.

FR-TIM-009.reasoning: The window is real and enforced: it opens at the dip confirmation, runs a fixed 180 seconds in real time across backgrounding and locking, and its expiry produces a blocking alert, an invalidated status and a recovery conversation that prevents continuation with the spent kit — with one warning given mid-window. Three gaps keep it from full. The invalidation can be reversed by an unverified self-report that the stick never left its wrapping, declaring the kit valid again on the user's word alone. The window does not survive a process restart: a killed and relaunched app forgets the dipped stick entirely, on both platforms, so the invalidation never happens for exactly the user most likely to return late. And quitting mid-window through the cancellation alert leaves no invalidation or record at all, so abandonment escapes the rule that expiry enforces.

FR-TIM-008.reasoning: The minimum cannot be beaten by the user on either platform: the control that opens the scanner is locked for the first seventy seconds, and capture is withheld until the full minimum inside the scanner, so no image can predate the colour-evolution period however the user behaves. Demonstration mode is exempt on both platforms, as the requirement demands. Caveats that stop short of a breach: the prevention is entirely silent, leaving the user up to five seconds of apparently scanning while nothing is captured; on one platform the pre-minimum frames are handed to a component whose internal handling cannot be read, though the observed rule — results only from post-minimum images — holds; and what demonstration mode means for the maximum window differs by platform, which is FR-TIM-011's edge rather than this requirement's.

FR-TIM-011.reasoning: Scanning is genuinely confined to the window: both bounds are fixed in the build, the window is checked on every scanner entry and across backgrounding, retries are allowed inside it and refused after it, and expiry invalidates the attempt with a blocking alert and new-kit troubleshooting. Four things keep it from full. The platforms disagree where the window closes — at capture or at result — so a slow analysis is silently logged a failure on one platform only. Deadline detection on one platform is frame-driven, so a stalled camera means the expiry is never noticed inside the scanner. In demonstration mode one platform applies no deadline and the other a shortened one, two readings of a silence the corpus never resolves. And the window is measured on the user-movable device clock, FR-TIM-004's unimplemented business, judged at the framework feature.

FR-TIM-005.reasoning: Half the requirement is delivered, imperfectly, for one stage. The wait after dipping shows a count to the moment scanning is permitted, as a number and a fill, singular and plural handled, and correct across leaving and returning; but the figure is seventy-five units over seventy real seconds, so the displayed time is not time. The other half, time remaining before the window expires, is displayed nowhere: once the count ends the button shows only its action label while roughly two thirds of the three-minute window is still running, and the sole mention of expiry is one fixed ninety-second sentence that is right only if it appears on schedule. The other timed stages have no display at all: the fifteen-minute sample window is checked silently, and the post-scan waits show an animation with no figure.

FR-TIM-014.reasoning: Neither platform ever schedules a local notification for any timing purpose: nothing arms a notification, alarm or scheduled work when the application goes to the background mid-window, verified as an absence on both platforms. The notifications the product does post carry support and consultation messages. What the user gets instead is an in-app alert on return, after the window has already lapsed, which is later than the requirement wants and reaches only users who return unprompted.

FR-COM-009.reasoning: This requirement supplies the mechanism for FR-TIM-014, locally generated notifications that need no backend connectivity, and no such mechanism exists for timing on either platform. The product's general notification machinery is proven to work, since support and consultation messages use it, so what is missing is not the capability but any connection between it and the timing windows.

FR-COM-012.reasoning: Two of the three clauses hold. The permission is requested, with the software's own message shown before the platform prompt and refusal honoured without asking the system; and refusal blocks nothing, since no step of the test consults the permission. The explanation clause fails in substance: the message is a generic reassurance that never says what the notifications are for, and the purpose the corpus wants the permission for, timing warnings, is not among the purposes the product's notifications actually serve. The whole ask also sits behind a remote switch, so even the requesting clause holds only as configuration currently stands.

FR-TIM-012.reasoning: Each obligation is delivered somewhere, and neither is delivered where the requirement puts it. The user is always told the test is over, promptly, wherever they are, even returning from an interruption, and the alert's only exit leads to an explanation. But the reason is in the invalidation message itself only for the sample expiry; for the stick timeout it arrives one screen later, and for the server-declared invalid stick a screen later again, behind a generic title. The instruction to repeat the test with a new kit exists nowhere at invalidation time: the spent-kit branch says the kit cannot be reused and routes to support, the sample-expiry alert offers to send a new kit, and the plain statement that a new kit is required appears only on the next attempt within twenty-four hours. Nothing anywhere says to repeat the test. The product also deliberately departs from the requirement's blanket instruction where the kit was never opened, truthfully telling the user it is still valid, and it cannot state a reason for the one invalidation whose grounds only the server knows. The requirement needs amending before it can be specified against, which the candidates below propose.

FR-FLW-009.reasoning: The mechanism exists and behaves as required in every respect but the one the requirement leads with: the card never displays the time remaining. During the wait after dipping the flow itself opens the content, the content is a genuine function of elapsed time at thresholds fixed in the application, all of it is optional, and it yields the instant the user may act; those clauses are met in full. But the remaining time lives in a separate countdown control beside the card rather than in it, and that control shows a distorted count; the card's only statement of time is one fixed sentence that is right only on schedule; and the waits after the scan get a card with no figure and no time-driven change at all. Two rulings are needed to close the judgement: whether a card plus an adjacent countdown satisfies a requirement written as one card, and whether indeterminate waits on the system count as timed waiting periods. The thresholds clause is also met only per build, since the two platforms ship different values and one varies them by language.

checked_against.label: Rev 1.24 · Epic Map Rev 1.18
checked_against.why_this_matters: Every coverage verdict in this file — covered, partly, uncovered — is relative to this revision. A later revision may already have closed a gap this file reports.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: The screen stays awake for the whole test, so the countdown is never hidden by the lock screen.
uncovered_behaviours.why: Keeping the screen awake for the whole test is what makes the countdown and the timed messages actually visible, and no requirement in the corpus mentions the display's sleep behaviour at all; without it the timed flow would spend most of its life behind the lock screen.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: The troubleshooting chat asks whether the stick was removed from its wrapping and offers YES / NO answers.
uncovered_behaviours.why: Asking whether the stick ever left its wrapping, with two answers leading to different fates for the kit, is recovery logic no timing requirement contemplates; it exists because the deadline can expire before anything was physically spent, a case the corpus never addresses.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: An expired attempt is recorded as timed out and, in this build, whatever was captured is still uploaded for review.
uncovered_behaviours.why: Marking the order timed out and still uploading whatever was captured is data handling the timing requirements never mention; the invalidated attempt has an afterlife — review, reporting, kit consequences — that no corpus requirement currently owns.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: The timed-out attempt, with whatever images exist, is still uploaded for quality review; the user is not told.
uncovered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-011 says invalidate; ACR additionally keeps whatever images exist and uploads the timed-out attempt for quality review without telling the user. No requirement covers retaining or transmitting the data of a failed attempt, so behaviour with real privacy and expectation consequences currently has no home in the corpus.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: The screen stays awake during the wait, so the countdown remains visible without touching the phone.
uncovered_behaviours.why: Keeping the screen awake is what makes a glanceable countdown work, and no requirement asks for it; the timing requirements assume the display stays visible without saying how. A candidate raised with an earlier epic's review already proposes this rule, so it is recorded here without a new one.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: How long after dipping the user tapped SCAN is recorded in analytics, not shown to the user.
uncovered_behaviours.why: The time between dipping and scanning is measured and reported for analytics but never shown or kept with the test. It is the very quantity the timing windows exist to bound, and the corpus is silent about a measurement the product already makes.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: Leaving the chat by back or close asks "Quit the test?" / "Are you sure you want to leave?" with Quit and Stay.
uncovered_behaviours.why: Nothing in the corpus states whether the explanation of a failed test may be abandoned or what confirms leaving it; the exit confirmation here is inherited flow behaviour, with the platforms differing in button casing.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: Support, reached from the chat, ends the test; when the support screen closes the user is returned home.
uncovered_behaviours.why: Where support leads after it closes is not covered by any requirement; recorded because for a timed-out test the support screen is the end of the flow, with home behind it.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: When time runs out in the camera, whatever was captured is uploaded silently as a timed-out attempt; the user is not told.
uncovered_behaviours.why: Nothing in the corpus says whether a timed-out attempt's captured data is kept, transmitted or discarded; the product transmits it in the background without telling the user, which Product should adopt or reject deliberately rather than inherit.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: When time runs out on the instructions screen before scanning, nothing is uploaded; only the timeout status is kept on the device.
uncovered_behaviours.why: A timeout before any scan leaves only a local record and the backend is never told; no requirement addresses reporting invalidations, which is why a candidate below asks for it.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: Returning to the troubleshooting chat after 15+ minutes away restarts the app on iOS but leaves the chat in place on Android.
uncovered_behaviours.why: Once the test is invalidated no requirement protects the explanation screen itself, and the platforms disagree: a long absence on that screen restarts one platform and leaves the other in place, so whether the reason survives the user's absence is currently chance.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: Arrival of the ready and expiry messages, and video replays, are reported to analytics.
uncovered_behaviours.why: Whether the ready and expiry messages were reached, and whether the video was replayed, is already measured by the product; no requirement addresses instrumentation of the wait.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: If the upload wait exceeds 45 seconds, an alert "Connectivity Issue" interrupts with a message about checking the internet connection and OK.
uncovered_behaviours.why: A fixed interval guards the upload wait and interrupts it with a connectivity alert; no requirement asks for a stalled wait to be noticed at all, so the guard, its threshold and its wording are all unspecified.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: If the phone has no internet at the 45-second mark, "No Internet Connection" is shown instead, and OK returns to the wait.
uncovered_behaviours.why: The guard distinguishes an absent connection from a transfer that is failing and words the alert accordingly; nothing in the corpus asks the software to tell those cases apart.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: On Android only, a second timeout while the result is already queued for the clinician skips the alert and proceeds to results.
uncovered_behaviours.why: One platform ends the wait silently and proceeds to results when the result is already queued for the clinician, while the other always alerts. No requirement covers ending a wait without telling the user, and a specification should not inherit this divergence by accident.

uncovered_behaviours.behaviour: The 45 seconds count only while the analysis screen is in front; time spent away pauses the threshold.
uncovered_behaviours.why: The guard counts only time spent with the wait on screen, so time away does not trigger it; no requirement says how a wait's guard should treat absence.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: After dipping, a button counts down '75 SECONDS TO GO' and turns into SCAN when it reaches zero.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-001 asks only that a minimum duration exist; ACR goes further and shows it as a live countdown, which is the first half of FR-TIM-005 — the time remaining until the next action is permitted — delivered prominently. The second half of FR-TIM-005, time remaining before the window expires, appears nowhere.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The countdown shows 75 seconds but runs for 70 real seconds, so SCAN appears about five seconds before 75 have passed.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The displayed minimum and the enforced minimum deliberately differ: 75 counted units elapse in 70 real seconds so the user reaches the camera as the stick becomes scannable. FR-TIM-001's minimum is enforced downstream at the true value, but the display FR-TIM-005 would rely on does not measure real seconds.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Once SCAN appears the user has until 180 seconds after dipping to finish scanning; no on-screen clock shows the time left.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The permitted completion window FR-TIM-001 requires exists — from the minimum to 180 seconds after the start event — but once the countdown ends nothing shows how much of it remains, so FR-TIM-005's display of time before expiry is absent exactly where it would matter.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: About 90 seconds after dipping a chat bubble says 'Click Scan now. The stick will expire in 90 seconds.'
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The only statement of remaining time the user ever gets is a scripted sentence timed to be true when it appears; FR-TIM-005 asks for a display of the time remaining before the window expires, and a fixed phrase that would silently become false if the window or pacing changed is at best a stand-in for one.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: When results are produced successfully the stick clock is cleared; the next test starts a fresh clock.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-002 says the start time shall be recorded and persistently retained but not when the record may end; ACR's answer — discard at success, fresh clock for the next test — is a reasonable reading the requirement never states.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The alert's only button reads 'Continue' on iOS and 'CONTINUE' on Android.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The expiry behaviour is the same in substance on both platforms, but the one word every timed-out user reads is cased differently on each; trivial, yet it is a visible seam in what FR-TIM-001 treats as one defined behaviour.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Tapping the button opens a troubleshooting chat headed STICK NO LONGER VALID explaining that more than 3 minutes have passed since dipping.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Expiry opens a guided recovery that states the reason — more than three minutes since the dip — which is FR-TIM-012's informing done well; the conversation that follows goes beyond anything FR-TIM-001's 'expiry behaviour' or FR-TIM-012's instruction describes.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The expiry alert can interrupt the instructions chat and the camera; on Android it can also interrupt the analysis screen.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The platforms disagree about where the permitted completion window ends: one closes it when capture completes and lets a long analysis finish, the other keeps enforcing it into analysis and can fail a test whose images are already taken. FR-TIM-001's 'defined window' and FR-TIM-011's expiry thus have two ends, one per platform.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If the system kills the app mid-wait, Android restores the countdown and deadline; iOS forgets the dip and restarts from the home screen.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-002's persistent retention exists on one platform only: one writes the start to durable storage and can restore the countdown and deadline after a system kill, the other holds it in memory and forgets the dip entirely — half the product meets the requirement and half does not.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If the user force-quits and relaunches mid-wait, both apps open at the home screen with no memory that a stick was dipped.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: After a force-quit both platforms present a home screen with no memory of the dipped stick — one because nothing was persisted, the other because the persisted start is wiped as the home screen appears.
