FR-TIM-002's retention is thus defeated even where it exists, and FR-STA-007's identify-and-invalidate on reopening has nothing to work from on either platform.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Coming back after more than 15 minutes away normally restarts the app from the beginning, but not while a stick clock is running.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Suppressing the idle restart while the clock runs is FR-STA-003's no-inactivity-timeout term honoured for this stage; partly, because the corpus makes a test active from the control that starts it, and the same protection is denied to the earlier stages of the same active test.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The scanning-stage bubbles keep pace with real time even if the user leaves the app, so 'expire in 90 seconds' stays roughly accurate.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The scripted timing copy stays roughly truthful because pacing follows real time rather than time in the foreground, which is FR-TIM-003's derivation applied to content; but FR-STA-002 forbids delivering instructional content while backgrounded and asks for resumption from the point reached, and one platform keeps scheduling items while suspended, so the two platforms resume by different rules.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: All stage clocks read the phone's clock; setting it forward expires the stick early and setting it back extends the window.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-004 requires a time source the user cannot move; every stage clock in ACR reads the device's wall clock, so setting it forward expires the stick early and setting it back extends the window indefinitely. Nothing of the requirement's substance is delivered — its own notes record it as future development, and ACR is the state those notes describe.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Changing only the time zone does not affect any clock; the app compares absolute instants, not local times.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The time-zone half of FR-TIM-004 is genuinely met: both platforms compare absolute instants, so changing the zone moves nothing. Only the clock half — the one with teeth — is unmet, which makes this the one corner of the requirement ACR already satisfies.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Expiry is noticed only when a screen checks; nothing fires while the app is closed — no alarm, no notification.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Deriving elapsed time on return satisfies FR-TIM-003's letter, and the requirement demands nothing proactive; but the consequence is that expiry is only ever noticed when a screen looks — no alarm or notification exists — so the user who stays away learns of the expiry only by coming back.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The 180-second and 75-second values exist only because this build overrides the product-wide defaults of 120 and 60 seconds.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The values are fixed in the application as FR-TIM-001 requires, but 'the application' is one variant of a family: the same code carries different defaults that this product overrides, so the fixed values are per-variant facts a release engineer sets, not constants of the product's design.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: On iOS, after an analysis fails for a non-quality reason, the next test that session may run without the Time Is Up cutoff.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: A static reading of one platform suggests the expiry mechanism may not be re-armed for the next test after certain failures, silently removing FR-TIM-001's defined expiry behaviour for that run; unconfirmed at runtime, but a defined behaviour that can lapse without trace is a defect in the very definition the requirement asks for.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Within the limit, tapping DIPPED IT starts the stick clock and the 75-second countdown as usual.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-006 defines only the failure side — prevent and explain when the limit is exceeded; the within-limit case, where the confirmation passes straight through into the next timed stage, is the requirement's unstated complement rather than anything it asks for.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The sample check exists only in the US build; other builds of the same product skip it entirely.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The requirement is unconditional: the software shall measure and enforce the sample age limit. In ACR the entire check exists only in the US build of the product and other variants skip it, so the requirement describes one build's behaviour, not the software's.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The alert also says this kit can no longer be used and offers to send a new one.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The explanation goes beyond FR-TIM-006's error message into FR-TIM-012's ground: the user is told the reason and that this kit is finished, and a new kit is promised. FR-TIM-012 asks for an instruction to repeat the test with a new kit; ACR instead offers to send one, which commits the backend to a remedy the requirement never mentions.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The attempt is recorded as 'sample expired', and afterwards the app treats this kit as used up.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Recording the attempt as an expired sample and treating the kit as spent goes beyond FR-TIM-006's wording, which stops at preventing and explaining; but that durable record is the material FR-KIT-007 depends on when the next test attempt must be met with a message matched to the previous test's outcome.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: After Support, the user lands back on the home screen rather than in the test.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: That the user lands at the home screen with no path back into the test makes FR-TIM-006's prevention permanent, but the requirement says nothing about where the user goes after the error, so the routing is ACR's own resolution of a question the corpus leaves open.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If the app is killed after CUP IS FULL, iOS forgets the tap and the check is skipped; Android keeps the time on disk.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-002 requires the start time of each time-dependent stage to be persistently retained. Android retains this one on disk; iOS holds it only in memory, so if the process dies before the completion tap the freshness check silently disappears and an old sample passes — the safeguard FR-TIM-006 asks for stops existing exactly when it is hardest to notice.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Being away for more than 15 minutes before dipping restarts the app from the home screen, so the expiry alert is rarely reached that way.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-STA-003 forbids any inactivity timeout while a test is active, and a test is active from the control that starts it; ACR still applies its idle restart at this stage because no stick clock runs yet. The restart shares the 15-minute threshold, so most users who exceed the sample limit while away meet the home screen instead of FR-TIM-006's explanatory error.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: At exactly 15 minutes iOS still allows dipping; Android already treats the sample as expired.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-006 speaks of one defined limit, but at exactly the limit the platforms disagree — one still accepts the sample, the other already rejects it. Practically invisible, yet it means the limit's own definition differs between the two implementations of the same rule.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Setting the phone's clock back extends the 15 minutes; setting it forward shortens them.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-004 requires elapsed time to come from a source the user cannot move; both platforms measure this window on the device's wall clock, so setting the clock back extends the limit and setting it forward shortens it. Nothing of the requirement is delivered — its own notes record it as future development, and ACR is the state those notes describe.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Before the alert, no chat bubble or screen mentions the 15-minute rule; the alert is the first the user hears of it.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Silence while timing is what FR-TIM-006's note asks for, but ACR extends it further than the note requires: the limit is never mentioned anywhere until it is broken, so the first the user hears of the rule is the alert that ends their kit — a product choice the requirement neither asks for nor forbids.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Tapping DIPPED IT starts one three-minute test clock; the SCAN control appears at once below the chat, locked, showing a countdown.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-007 asks that the release instruction be presented only after the residence time has elapsed; ACR presents the control immediately but locked, counting down, so the instruction is withheld in effect though visible from the first second. The countdown itself is the display FR-TIM-005 requires of the time remaining until the next action is permitted.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The countdown starts at "75 SECONDS TO GO" and reaches zero after about 70 real seconds.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The stated residence time is 75 seconds but the control unlocks after 70, the displayed count running about seven percent fast to hide the difference; FR-TIM-007's 'only after the residence time has elapsed' is met five seconds short, deliberately, as a head start for opening the camera, and FR-TIM-005's displayed remaining time is not measured in real seconds.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: A coloured fill sweeps across the control as it counts; at zero the label becomes SCAN and the control becomes tappable.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The unlock — the fill completing, the label changing, the control becoming tappable — is ACR's presentation of the release instruction, so FR-TIM-007's gated moment exists and is unmistakable; but it arrives at the shortened seventy seconds rather than after the stated residence time, so the letter of 'only after' is not quite kept.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: During the wait nine timed messages arrive: why the wait is needed, a scanning demo video, distance advice, then "We're ready. Let's scan."
partly_covered_behaviours.why: What fills the wait is scripted narration with a demonstration video — content FR-TIM-007 never mentions. The corpus instead fills a timed wait with FR-IMG-022's practice scan, an interactive rehearsal of the scanning interaction; ACR's watch-only video is the ancestor of that idea, not its equal, so the waiting period's content is a departure the mapping should not blur.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: "We're ready. Let's scan." appears roughly 70 seconds after the dip, about when the control unlocks.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The 'ready' instruction lands at roughly the moment the control unlocks, which reads as FR-TIM-007 satisfied; but the message follows its own scripted pauses and nothing links it to the gate, so the instruction is presented near the elapsed time rather than because of it.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Roughly 90 seconds after the dip a reminder appears: "Click Scan now. The stick will expire in 90 seconds."
partly_covered_behaviours.why: A reminder half-way through the window goes beyond FR-TIM-009, which names only the invalidation; and as the sole statement of remaining time it is a fixed sentence that happens to be true at the moment it appears, not the live display of time before expiry that FR-TIM-005 requires.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Tapping SCAN records how long the user waited and opens the scanner; nothing else is checked at that moment.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Tapping the unlocked control records how long the user waited and reports the step — a slice of FR-ANL-001's required analytics of progress through the flow. The timing requirements themselves are silent here, and deliberately so: no check runs at this tap, because expiry would already have fired if the window had closed.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Troubleshooting says more than 3 minutes passed since dipping and asks whether the stick was taken out of its wrapping.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Naming the cause — more than three minutes since the dip — is FR-TIM-012's informing done properly; the follow-up question about whether the stick ever left its wrapping goes beyond both requirements, existing because the deadline can pass before the stick was ever exposed, a case the corpus does not contemplate.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: NO, I DID NOT EXTRACT IT marks the attempt a dry run, says the kit is still valid, and offers BACK TO HOME VIEW.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-009 says invalidate and prevent continuation; ACR lets the user reverse that verdict by answering that the stick never left its wrapping, whereupon the attempt becomes a dry run and the kit is declared valid, verified by nothing but the answer. A recovery the requirement does not contemplate, resting entirely on self-report.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: After the 90-second reminder there is no further warning before the alert; the clock simply runs out.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: After the single mid-window reminder the clock simply runs out, and the first the user hears of the expiry is the alert itself; FR-TIM-009 asks for exactly that invalidation and nothing more, so the absence of escalation is the requirement operating as written rather than a gap in it.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: That alert offers only SUPPORT; the attempt is recorded as an expired sample and the user goes to customer support.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The support-only exit is FR-SUP-003 working — the user cannot resolve an expired sample themselves, and support contact is the single action offered; recording the attempt as an expired sample goes beyond FR-TIM-006's wording, though it is what makes the failure durable rather than momentary.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Messages that fell due while the app was in the background appear all at once on Android; iOS has no catch-up step.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-STA-002 requires that instructional content not be delivered while the application is in the background and that delivery resume from the point reached; one platform resumes with a bulk catch-up of everything overdue, while the other keeps scheduling items even while suspended and its on-screen behaviour after a long absence is unconfirmed, so the two resume differently and only one clearly matches the requirement.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Choosing Quit ends the test and returns home; nothing is recorded about the dipped stick, and no failure is logged.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Of FR-STA-010's three obligations on a confirmed cancellation, two are met — the test cannot be resumed and the user returns to the start — but the third, invalidating the active test, never happens: the order's status is left untouched and no record exists that a dipped stick was abandoned, so the kit's fate is unwritten anywhere but analytics.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: While the clock is running, returning from the background never resets the app to its start screen, as it otherwise can.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-STA-003 forbids any inactivity timeout while a test is active, and while the stick clock runs ACR honours that: the idle restart is suppressed on both platforms. Partly, because a test is active from the control that starts it, and this protection begins only at the dip — the earlier stages of the same active test still lose to the idle reset.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: After the app is killed and relaunched, the dipped stick is forgotten: no deadline is enforced and a new test can start.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-002 requires the stage start to be retained persistently and FR-STA-007 requires a reopened app to identify and invalidate the incomplete test; one platform never persists the start, the other persists it and then wipes it at the home screen, and neither looks for the incomplete test at all — so a killed app forgets the dipped stick and a fresh test can begin as though nothing happened.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The chat says "wait 75 seconds", the countdown starts at 75, yet SCAN unlocks after 70; displayed seconds run about 7% fast.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The chat promises a 75-second wait, the counter starts at 75, and the gate opens after 70 real seconds because each displayed second lasts about 0.93; FR-TIM-005's displayed remaining time is therefore systematically wrong by design, and FR-TIM-007's residence time is shortened by the same five seconds the scanner later withholds from capture.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The "We're ready" message and the SCAN unlock are timed separately; neither triggers the other.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The 'ready' instruction and the unlock are two independent timelines tuned to coincide — scripted pauses on one side, the control's own schedule on the other, with nothing connecting them; FR-TIM-007's 'only after' is thus achieved by arithmetic that happens to agree today, and either side can drift without the other noticing.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: SCAN opens the scanner about 70 seconds after the dip; the scanner starts searching for the Color-Board immediately.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-008 prevents progression past the stage before the minimum has elapsed; ACR lets the user into the scanner five seconds early and starts searching at once, so the stage is enterable before the minimum even though capture — the act the requirement protects — is still withheld.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Each captured image is stamped with how many seconds had passed since the dip.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-011 asks that scanning be permitted only within the window; stamping every captured image with the seconds elapsed since the dip goes further, making compliance evidenced per image rather than merely enforced. No corpus requirement asks for that timing record, though downstream review of window compliance would rest on it.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Once the images are captured and analysis begins, the three-minute deadline no longer interrupts the user.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The requirement says the board may be scanned only within the window and the test invalidated when it expires; ACR reads 'scanned' as 'captured', so once the images exist the deadline stops interrupting the user even though the clock is still running. Where the window ends is thus ACR's interpretation, not the requirement's words.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Android notices the deadline only when an image result returns; iOS reacts the instant the clock ends.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Both platforms enforce the deadline, but one is told the instant the clock ends while the other only notices when the next processed frame returns; ordinarily a one-frame delay, but if frames stop arriving the expiry is never noticed inside the scanner on that platform, so the requirement's guarantee rests on the camera staying healthy.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: No too-early check exists at scanner entry; the 5-second gap is covered by withholding capture, not by a message.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The requirement's prevention holds, but nothing at scanner entry checks the minimum — the gap is closed silently in the capture path alone, with no message. The user is blocked without ever being told a block exists, and the enforcement lives in one place rather than at the doorway the user actually walks through.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Demo mode is entered by long-pressing the start button on the home screen, when the backend allows it or in debug builds.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-008 presumes a demonstration mode exists — it exempts one — but says nothing about how it is reached; ACR's answer is a hidden long press on the home screen, allowed in debug builds or when the backend permits it, which is behaviour the corpus neither requires nor constrains.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: In demo mode capture starts immediately on both platforms; only Android still enforces a deadline, 105 seconds after opening the scanner.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-008 lifts the minimum in demonstration mode and is silent about the completion window, as is FR-TIM-011; ACR's platforms resolved that silence differently — one applies no deadline at all in demo, the other still ends the demo scan after a shortened window — so the same words currently describe two behaviours.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Closing the scanner with its X returns to the chat; the clock keeps running and SCAN can be tapped again.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-011 says only when scanning is permitted, so ACR's answer — leave and re-enter the scanner as often as you like while the window lasts, with the clock untouched — is a consequence the requirement implies but never states: the window belongs to the stick, not to the attempt.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If analysis is still running when the deadline passes, Android records the test as timed out with no message; iOS records nothing.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The platforms disagree about what the window's expiry means once capture has succeeded but analysis is still running: one records the test as timed out silently, the other records nothing and lets the analysis finish. A slow but successful scan is a completed test on one platform and a logged failure on the other, so FR-TIM-011's 'invalidate' has two meanings at this edge.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: For up to 5 seconds the scanner can be open, framed and apparently scanning while nothing is captured.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: For up to five seconds the scanner is open, apparently working, and silently capturing nothing; FR-TIM-008's prevention holds, but FR-TIM-005 — which requires the time remaining until the next action is permitted to be displayed — would have this residue of the wait shown, and the scanner shows nothing but its normal framing guidance.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: After tapping DIPPED IT, a countdown button appears under the chat reading "75 SECONDS TO GO" and counts down.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-005 asks for two figures per timed stage: time until the next action is permitted and time until the window expires. The countdown that appears on dipping shows only the first, counting down to the moment scanning unlocks.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The count starts at 75 and reaches zero after about 70 real seconds, so each displayed second is slightly shorter than a real one.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The requirement asks for the time remaining, and what is displayed is seventy-five units spread over seventy real seconds, so the figure on screen is not time: it overstates what is left for the whole of the count and would fail a check against any watch.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: A coloured fill sweeps across the countdown button from left to right and reaches the far edge as the count ends.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The fill is a second, non-numeric rendering of the same count, so progress toward the permitted action is shown twice; it inherits the same scaled clock as the number beside it and adds nothing about expiry.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The wording switches to the singular "1 SECOND TO GO" for the last displayed second.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Grammatical care in the countdown's wording is part of displaying remaining time legibly, which is the requirement's subject; it still serves only the next-action half of it.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: When the count reaches zero the button reads "SCAN" and becomes tappable; tapping it opens the camera.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The count reaching zero is what permits the next action, so the display genuinely counts to the moment FR-TIM-005 names; the button being inert until then is also the early edge of FR-TIM-011's rule that scanning is permitted only within its window, whose late edge is enforced by the expiry alert elsewhere.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Time left before the stick expires is never shown as a figure; one fixed message "...will expire in 90 seconds" appears around 90 seconds.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The second figure FR-TIM-005 asks for, time before the window expires, is never displayed at all. Its only trace is one fixed sentence naming ninety seconds, scheduled by elapsed time rather than read from the clock, which is a message rather than a display and is wrong whenever it appears late.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: During the processing and upload waits after the scan, no time figure is shown; the waiting message carries a looping animation instead.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The waits after the scan show a looping animation and no figure. If they count as active time-dependent stages, FR-TIM-005's display is absent for them; and the waiting card FR-FLW-009 asks to display the time remaining shows activity instead. They are waits on the system rather than windows on the user, so whether either requirement was meant to reach them needs a Product ruling.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The 15-minute urine-sample window has no visible timer or warning; it is checked silently when DIPPED IT is tapped.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The fifteen-minute sample window is exactly the kind of stage the requirement describes: an action is permitted only within a window. Neither the window's existence nor its remaining time is ever displayed; the first the user learns of it is when it has already been missed.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Leaving the app during the countdown does not pause it; on return the count shows the correct remaining value.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The displayed time stays truthful across leaving and returning because it is recomputed from the recorded start rather than resumed from where it paused, which is the arithmetic FR-TIM-003 requires after any interruption. FR-TIM-005 says nothing about interruptions; this is the behaviour its display needs anyway.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If the count finished while the app was away, the button already reads "SCAN" on return.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: A count that finished while the user was away is shown already finished on return, so stale remaining time is never displayed; still only the next-action half of the requirement.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: No reminder, banner or system notification is raised when the count ends or the stick nears expiry while the app is in the background.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Both requirements exist for exactly this moment, a window nearing its end while the application is in the background, and nothing is delivered: neither platform has any path that schedules a local notification, alarm or reminder for timing, verified as an absence on both. The user finds out only by returning.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If the full 180-second window passes while the app is away, the "Time Is Up" alert appears as soon as the app returns.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: What the product actually does about a window lapsing in the background is tell the user on return, in the foreground, after the fact. FR-TIM-014 asks to be told before the lapse, while still away; the on-return alert is the substitute, and it reaches only users who come back.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If the app is killed mid-countdown, Android still knows when the stick was dipped; iOS forgets the dip and the countdown.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-STA-007, owned by the state-retention feature but squarely on point here, turns on the software recognising an incomplete test when reopened after being killed, and FR-TIM-002 requires each stage start time to be persistently retained. One platform retains the moment the stick was dipped and the other holds it only in memory, and neither uses what it has to invalidate or inform, so the substrate both requirements depend on is half present at best.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: On the home screen the app first shows its own message "We're here to help" asking to allow notifications, with OK and No Thanks.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: An explanation does precede the platform prompt, as the requirement asks, but it is a generic reassurance that never says why notifications are wanted, which is the substance of that clause.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The explanation is shown once per install and skipped when the system has already granted or denied notifications.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Asking once per install and skipping the explanation once the system has an answer respects platform norms and breaches nothing in the text; whether a user who refused is ever approached again is not derivable, and the requirement is silent on it too.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The whole notification ask can be switched off remotely by a feature flag.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The entire ask can be switched off remotely, so whether the software requests the permission at all is settled by configuration rather than by the software; the requirement reads as unconditional, and the production state of the switch is not derivable.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The explanation never mentions test timing; the notifications it asks for carry support and consultation messages.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The permission infrastructure exists to carry support and consultation messages, not timing. The corpus ties this permission to the timing notification's needs, and an explanation written for a different purpose cannot explain the purpose the corpus wants the permission for; it is also further evidence that no timing notification exists to be permitted.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Tapping SCAN late, even after the 90-second warning, still opens the camera; only the 180-second expiry blocks the test.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-011 permits scanning only within the validated window and invalidates after it. Seen from this feature, the window's end is the only gate there is: the ninety-second warning does not block, and a late tap short of three minutes still opens the camera, which matches the requirement's shape. The enforcement itself belongs to the scanning-window feature.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The chat says "wait 75 seconds" and the button counts 75, but the button unlocks after 70 real seconds.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The copy promises seventy-five seconds, the display counts seventy-five, and seventy real seconds govern, so the one place remaining time is displayed it is displayed wrong; flagged by the extraction as behaviour not to copy.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Three minutes after the dip tap, if no scan has completed, a full-screen alert titled "Time Is Up" interrupts whatever the user is doing.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The user is informed promptly that the test is over, wherever they are in the flow, which is the requirement's premise; but the alert names neither the reason nor what to do next, which are the two things the requirement actually asks for at this moment.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The alert body reads "You can no longer use the stick for this test." It states the consequence, not why.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Consequence without reason: the body says the stick can no longer be used, not why. The reason the requirement wants in the invalidation message arrives only on the following screen.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The alert offers one button, "Continue" on iOS and "CONTINUE" on Android; it cannot be dismissed any other way.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The extraction left this line unmapped, but the dismissal mechanics serve the informing duty: the single undismissable button is the only exit and it leads to the screen that states the reason, so the reason is guaranteed to be presented eventually. The platforms differ only in the button's casing.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Tapping the button opens a chat headed "STICK NO LONGER VALID" that finally states the reason: more than 3 minutes since dipping.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The reason is delivered in full, more than three minutes since dipping, but one screen after the invalidation message rather than in it, which is where the requirement places it.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The chat then asks "did you extract the stick from its wrapping?" with "YES, I EXTRACTED THE STICK" and "NO, I DID NOT EXTRACT IT".
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The extraction read this as outside the requirement, but the triage question decides when the requirement's own instruction applies: only the answer that the stick was extracted leads to the new-kit branch. The requirement presumes every timing invalidation consumes the kit; the product first asks whether it actually did.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Answering yes shows "ORDER NEW KIT": the kit is single-use and cannot be reused; the only button is "TO CUSTOMER SUPPORT".
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The spent-kit branch tells the user the kit is single-use and cannot be reused, and routes to support, which also delivers FR-SUP-003's promise for a condition the user cannot resolve; but it never instructs them to repeat the test, so the requirement's instruction clause is half-delivered at best.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Answering no shows "KIT IS VALID", reassures the kit is still usable, and "BACK TO HOME VIEW" returns home with no failure recorded.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The requirement instructs a new kit on every timing invalidation; here the product deliberately tells the user the opposite, that the unopened kit is still valid, and records no failure. The branch is sensible and truthful, and a literal reading of the requirement would forbid it, which is a tension for Product to resolve rather than a defect.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Unless the server has switched this variant to single-kit mode, the yes/no answer is kept only on the device and the server is not told.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-KIT-004's reuse detection turns on the backend knowing a kit identifier has been used. As this variant ships, the answer to the consumed-kit question never leaves the device, so a kit spent by a timeout before any scan is invisible to that detection and would look fresh if presented again.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If the dip button is tapped more than 15 minutes after confirming the urine sample, "Urine sample expired" appears and the timer never starts.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: This is the shape FR-TIM-006 asks for on the equivalent stage of the new device: the elapsed time from sample confirmation is measured, the user is prevented from proceeding, and the message is explanatory. For FR-TIM-012 the alert names the rule that was broken, unlike the stick timeout, but no instruction to repeat the test follows.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Its body says the sample must be tested within 15 minutes, this kit can no longer be used, and a new one will be sent.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The fullest invalidation message in the product: the rule, the consequence, and the kit's replacement all in one alert. It is still phrased as an offer to send a new kit rather than an instruction to repeat the test with one, which is the closest the product comes to the requirement's second clause.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The only button is "Support" ("SUPPORT" on Android); there is no troubleshooting chat and no way to continue or go home directly.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: A support-only exit fits FR-SUP-003, since an expired sample is nothing the user can fix; the requirement under map does not prescribe the exit, and the alert's single route means the user cannot decline the conversation and simply go home.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: After a sample expiry, only Android warns "This kit has been used" on the next attempt; iOS starts the new test without comment.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-KIT-007's twenty-four-hour gate exists to catch the next attempt after an invalidated test, and after a sample expiry it fires on one platform and not on the other, because only one records the failure. The same timing failure thus produces different warnings on the next attempt depending on the phone in hand.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Nothing warns the user that the 15-minute sample window is running or about to lapse before they tap dip.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The sample window is an active time-dependent stage whose remaining time FR-TIM-005 requires to be displayed, and nothing displays it or even reveals it exists; the first the user hears of the window is its failure. The requirement is owned by the timing-display feature; this line is the invalidation-side view of the same absence.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If the 3 minutes lapse while scanning, the camera stops and "Time Is Up" appears over it, leading to the same chat.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The window lapsing mid-scan stops the capture and informs the user, which is FR-TIM-011's invalidation enforced inside the camera; the message is the same reason-less alert, so FR-TIM-012's gaps repeat here unchanged.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Once a scan has succeeded and analysis begins, a lapsing timer produces no message at all; the analysis simply continues.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-011's invalidation clause reads as unconditional, yet once a capture has succeeded the lapsing window is ignored and the result is delivered. Whether a window that expires after a successful capture invalidates is a boundary the requirement does not state, and the product answers it silently.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If analysis rejects the scan and returns the user to the camera after the window lapsed, "Time Is Up" appears immediately on re-entry.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The retry path honours the expired window: re-entering the camera after a rejected attempt is blocked at once when the window has lapsed, which enforces FR-TIM-011, and the user learns only then that the retry window had already closed; the alert again gives no reason.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: When the server reports the stick was not properly dipped, "Test Results Problem" replaces results: "Your stick and kit are no longer valid for use."
partly_covered_behaviours.why: If a stick the server declares dry is a timing failure, this is an invalidation on timing grounds delivered with a generic title and a body that states only invalidity: neither the reason nor any next step is in the message, the same displacement as the stick timeout.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: That alert gives neither a reason nor a next step; the explanation about patches not dipped comes only in the chat after the button.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The reason, patches not properly dipped, is again delivered one screen after the invalidation message, behind the alert's single button.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The dry-stick chat says the kit and stick are no longer valid and offers only "TO CUSTOMER SUPPORT"; there is no way to retest.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The user is told the kit and stick are no longer valid and routed to support, which fits FR-SUP-003 for a condition they cannot resolve; the requirement's instruction to repeat the test with a new kit is absent, as everywhere.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Whether a dry stick counts as a timing failure is decided by the server; the app only relays the verdict.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The requirement turns on the words 'invalidated on timing grounds', and for this invalidation the grounds live at the server: the application only relays a verdict it cannot explain. Whether a dry stick counts as timing, and whether the app can ever state its reason, needs a Product ruling.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Backgrounding during the 3-minute window does not pause the clock; if it lapsed while away, "Time Is Up" shows as soon as the app returns.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The invalidation message survives an interruption: the window keeps running against the recorded start and the alert is presented the moment the user returns, with the same content gaps it has in the foreground.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: No notification, sound or badge is sent while the app is in the background; the user learns of the timeout only by returning.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The moment FR-TIM-014 exists for, the window ending while the user is away, passes in silence: no notification, sound or badge on either platform, verified as an absence. The foreground alert on return is the only delivery vehicle the product has. The requirement is owned by the timing-display feature; this is the invalidation-side view of the same absence.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If the app is fully relaunched during the window, no timing message ever appears; the test starts over from home with the same kit.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: A relaunch during the window is the case FR-STA-007 describes, reopening after termination during an active test, and none of its three obligations is delivered: nothing identifies the lapsed test, nothing invalidates it, and no message ever appears, so the same kit is treated as fresh. FR-TIM-002's persistently retained start time exists on one platform only and is discarded on arrival home, which is why nothing can be said. Both requirements are owned elsewhere; this line is where their absence becomes a reusable dipped stick.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The stick window is 3 minutes from the dip tap; the on-screen countdown covers only 75 seconds, after which the button reads "SCAN".
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The displayed count covers only the first seventy-five units of a three-minute window, so most of the invalidation window runs with no display at all; FR-TIM-005's expiry half, owned by the timing-display feature, is the missing piece this boundary exposes.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Before time runs out the chat warns "Click Scan now. The stick will expire in 90 seconds." — the only advance warning of invalidation.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The only advance warning of invalidation anywhere is one scheduled sentence in the foreground chat. It is the nearest thing the product has to the expiry display FR-TIM-005 wants and to the about-to-expire warning FR-TIM-014 wants, and it is neither: fixed text rather than a reading of the clock, and foreground only.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Within 24 hours of a timeout where the stick was extracted, starting again shows "This kit has been used" with support and new-kit buttons.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The gate FR-KIT-007 requires exists and fires within twenty-four hours of a timeout where the stick was extracted, with a message and a confirmation of holding a new kit. It is also where the new-kit statement FR-TIM-012 wanted at invalidation is actually delivered, one attempt later than the requirement places it.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Choosing the new-kit option opens a "New Test" page: "A new kit is required" — the clearest statement anywhere that retesting needs a new kit.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The plainest statement in the product that a new kit is required exists on a dedicated page, reached from the used-kit warning on the next attempt; FR-TIM-012's instruction is therefore in the product but two taps and one attempt away from the moment the requirement names.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: That warning asks rather than blocks: after acknowledging it the test proceeds and nothing checks that a new kit is actually used.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Confirmation without verification is what FR-KIT-007's text asks, and the corpus accepts that because FR-KIT-004 is meant to catch actual reuse at the scan; but that catch depends on the backend knowing the kit was consumed, which a timeout before any scan never tells it, so for these kits the confirmation is the only control there is.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: If the user said they never extracted the stick, the next attempt shows no warning and the same kit is treated as fresh.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Read literally, FR-KIT-007's gate should fire after any invalidated test within the window; the product exempts the case where the user said the stick was never extracted and treats the kit as fresh, a deliberate exception the corpus does not have and should either adopt or overrule.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: All timing windows run on the device clock; changing the phone's time changes when a test is invalidated.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: FR-TIM-004 requires a time source the user cannot move, and every window here runs on the device clock, so changing the phone's time changes when a test is invalidated. The requirement is owned by the timers feature; this is the invalidation consequence of not having it.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Right after DIPPED IT, the user's own line "The stick was dipped and placed on the Color-Board." and a SCANNING header appear above the countdown.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The wait's content is opened by the flow itself: the echoed confirmation and a section header appear unbidden the moment the timed wait begins, which is the required shape, presented by the flow rather than fetched by the user. No time is shown yet.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Over the next 70 seconds, eight messages arrive one at a time, each after a typing indicator, at intervals fixed in the app.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Content that changes as the period elapses is delivered as messages appended one at a time at intervals fixed in the application, meeting the changing-content and fixed-thresholds clauses; nothing in the sequence displays the time remaining, which is the clause the same sentence of the requirement leads with.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The messages move from reassurance and an explanation of the wait, through scanning tips, to "We're ready. Let's scan." as the count ends.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The content is a genuine function of elapsed time, moving from reassurance through preparation to readiness just as the wait ends, which is exactly the mechanism the requirement describes; the remaining-time display is absent throughout.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The fifth message is a short video showing how to scan, with a "replay" control the user may ignore.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Instructional content placed inside the wait, with a replay the user may ignore: the card is used to teach, which the requirement permits since its content belongs to the approved content set, and ignoring the video costs nothing.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: About 20 seconds after "We're ready", a last message "Click Scan now. The stick will expire in 90 seconds." appears if unscanned.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The only content that ever states remaining time, and it is a fixed sentence scheduled by elapsed time rather than a display read from a clock, so it is correct only when nothing has delayed it.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Each message arrives with its own sound; iOS turns sound on when the instructions open, Android keeps the user's last mute choice.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The wait's messages are voiced, so the card is part of the spoken flow FR-FLW-008 governs, and that requirement says a silenced flow stays silent for the remainder of the test. One platform overrides the user's earlier silencing when this stage opens and the other honours it, so the clause holds on one platform only.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: After the scan a PROCESSING header and "Hold on while we analyze your scanned images." appear with a looping animation inside the bubble.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The post-scan wait gets a card presented by the flow, which is the required shape, but it displays no time and its content does not change as the period elapses; it shows activity instead.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: When the phone finishes analysing, "Done 🙂" appears and the animation plays out to its finished state.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The content changes once, on the event of finishing rather than as a function of elapsed time; telling the user the wait has ended is useful, but it is not the mechanism the requirement describes, and no figure is ever shown.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Then an ANALYZING header and "Fantastic. Please wait while we analyze your test results." appear with a looping animation during upload.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The upload wait repeats the same pattern: one message, a looping animation, no time, no time-driven change of content.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The waiting message's text never changes; only the animation loops, and no time figure is shown.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The longest wait in the flow never changes its content over time at all. Whether that breaches the requirement turns on its opening words: this wait is indeterminate rather than timed, so a Product ruling is needed on whether the card rule was meant to reach waits of unknown length.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Tapping OK restarts the 45-second wait with the same message; a second timeout offers "Retry" or "Support".
partly_covered_behaviours.why: A second timeout offers support alongside retry, which is FR-SUP-003's shape: the software cannot move forward and hands the user a way out. Whether one failed interval already counts as a condition the user cannot resolve themselves is a judgement the corpus does not make.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Choosing Support leaves the analysis wait and opens support.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Choosing support abandons the wait and reaches the support channel, which delivers FR-SUP-003's promise for this blocked state; the cost, that getting help ends the analysis wait, is not something the requirement weighs.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: After leaving and returning mid-wait, Android shows every overdue message at once and continues on schedule; iOS keeps its own schedule and may lag.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: Content as a function of elapsed time survives leaving and returning by design on one platform, which shows every overdue message at once and schedules the rest, and by chance on the other, where what appears depends on what the operating system allowed while away. A candidate raised with an earlier epic's review already covers delivery around backgrounding.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: Pacing differs slightly by platform: the first message lands 2.4 s (iOS) or 1 s (Android) after the header.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The thresholds are fixed in the application, as required, but fixed to different values on each platform, so the clause delivers consistency within one build and not between the two builds of the same product.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The Spanish build re-times the sequence on Android but not on iOS.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: One platform re-times the sequence for a second language and the other does not; the requirement fixes thresholds in the application without saying whether they may vary by language, and the product currently answers that question both ways.

partly_covered_behaviours.behaviour: The final expiry warning lands about 89 to 90 seconds after dipping, so its "90 seconds" is right only if on time.
partly_covered_behaviours.why: The one statement of remaining time is scheduled rather than computed, so its figure is right only when the message lands on time; flagged by the extraction as behaviour not to copy.

candidate_statements.statement: While a time-dependent stage of the test flow is active, the software shall prevent the device display from turning off.
candidate_statements.why: The countdown, the timed instructions and the expiry warning all live on the screen; if the display sleeps mid-wait the user loses every timing cue the corpus requires them to have, and on most devices the display would sleep well inside the three-minute window. ACR keeps the screen awake throughout the test on both platforms, and no corpus requirement mentions display sleep at all — the display requirements presume a screen that stays visible without saying so.
candidate_statements.note: Could join the timing-display feature's requirements rather than stand alone; scoping it to time-dependent stages rather than the whole session is deliberate, since ACR's whole-session approach is broader than the need.

candidate_statements.statement: When a test is invalidated on timing grounds, the software shall record the invalidation and its reason against the test, and shall treat the kit as no longer usable for testing.
candidate_statements.why: FR-TIM-006 stops at preventing and explaining, and FR-TIM-012 at informing and instructing; nothing requires the failed attempt to be written down or the kit spent. Yet FR-KIT-007's outcome-matched message on the next attempt, and any replacement-kit remedy promised to the user, both depend on that record existing. ACR records it deliberately on both platforms.
candidate_statements.note: Prefer amending FR-TIM-012, which already governs what happens at the moment of a timing invalidation, rather than adding a new requirement.

candidate_statements.statement: Following a timing invalidation, the software shall establish whether the reagent stick was exposed, and where the user confirms it was not, shall record the attempt as a test not performed and may permit the same kit to be used for a later test.
candidate_statements.why: FR-TIM-009 stops at invalidate-and-prevent, but the deadline can pass before the stick was ever exposed, and in that case nothing was actually spent. ACR resolves this with a recovery conversation whose second branch un-spends the kit on the user's word alone. Either that recovery is wanted — in which case it must be required, together with an explicit acceptance that the only verification is self-report — or it is not, in which case the current behaviour must be forbidden. The corpus currently does neither.
candidate_statements.note: Prefer amending FR-TIM-009, or folding into FR-TIM-012's recovery wording; the self-report-only verification is a Product decision that must be made in the open.

candidate_statements.statement: In demonstration mode the software shall apply none of the timing limits of this section, neither minimum durations nor permitted completion windows.
candidate_statements.why: FR-TIM-008 lifts only the minimum times in demonstration mode, and FR-TIM-011 says nothing about demonstration at all; ACR's two platforms resolved that silence in opposite directions, one applying no deadline in demo and the other a shortened one. Whichever answer Product wants, the corpus currently permits both at once.
candidate_statements.note: Prefer widening FR-TIM-008's demonstration-mode sentence to cover the whole timing section rather than adding a requirement.

candidate_statements.statement: The software shall record, with each captured image, the elapsed time since the start of the timed stage during which it was captured.
candidate_statements.why: The validated scanning window is enforced at capture but evidenced nowhere in the record the corpus asks for: the per-image record requirement covers camera parameters only, and nothing preserves proof that a given image fell inside the window. ACR stamps every image deliberately, and any downstream review of window compliance rests on that stamp.
candidate_statements.note: Could be an amendment to the existing per-image record requirement in the camera area rather than a new TIM requirement.

candidate_statements.statement: Where a test is invalidated on timing grounds after image capture has begun, the software shall transmit the captured images and their timing record to the backend for quality review, and the retention of that material shall be disclosed to the user.
candidate_statements.why: ACR uploads timed-out attempts, images and processing record included, on both platforms and never tells the user; the corpus neither requires nor forbids this, and data leaving the device from a test the user believes dead is a behaviour that must be either mandated or prohibited, not left unstated. The existing retention requirement only bounds data around a transmission it assumes was intended.
candidate_statements.note: Needs a Product decision on whether failed-attempt data may leave the device at all; the disclosure half may belong with the consent documents rather than the timing section. Touches the E04 candidate on discarding data of invalidated tests.

candidate_statements.statement: The software shall record the actual elapsed time of each timed stage of the test, and shall include those times in the data transmitted with the test.
candidate_statements.why: The timing windows exist because elapsed time bears on the validity of the result, and the shipping product already measures the interval between dipping and scanning, but reports it only to analytics; nothing requires the measured times to accompany the test record itself, where a clinician-facing system could use them.
candidate_statements.note: If the transmitted payload is specified under the data-transmission requirements, prefer adding it there rather than as a new TIM rule.

candidate_statements.statement: When a test is invalidated on timing grounds, the software shall state in the invalidation message itself which timing rule was not met, and shall instruct the user to repeat the test with a new kit where the kit has been consumed. Where the software establishes that the kit was not consumed, it shall state instead that the kit remains usable.
candidate_statements.why: The shipping product spreads the reason and the consequence over as many as three screens, never says to repeat the test, and has a branch the current requirement forbids by silence: a user who never opened the kit is truthfully told it is still usable. As written, FR-TIM-012 cannot be satisfied while keeping that sensible branch, so the departure should be decided rather than inherited.
candidate_statements.note: An amendment to FR-TIM-012 rather than a new requirement.

candidate_statements.statement: When a test is invalidated and the kit has been consumed, the software shall report the invalidation to the backend when connectivity permits, so that the consumed kit can be recognised if it is presented again.
candidate_statements.why: A kit spent by a timeout before any scan is unknown to the backend: the consumed-kit answer stays on the device, nothing is transmitted, and the confirmation gate on the next attempt asks rather than checks. The reuse detection the corpus relies on can therefore never fire for exactly the kits most likely to be presented again, and a relaunch during the window erases even the local record.
candidate_statements.note: An earlier epic's review proposed reporting the invalidation of tests ended by termination; cleaner as one rule covering every invalidation than as two.

candidate_statements.statement: The scanning-time window shall apply to the capture of the Test Board: a capture completed within the window shall remain valid although the window expires while analysis is in progress, and the software shall not invalidate the test on that ground.
candidate_statements.why: FR-TIM-011's invalidation clause reads as unconditional, but the shipping product lets the window lapse silently once a capture has succeeded and delivers the result. Either that is right and the requirement needs its boundary stated, or every analysis that outlives the window must be discarded, which is a different product; the choice should be made deliberately.
candidate_statements.note: Prefer amending FR-TIM-011, which the scanning-window feature owns; raised here because the silence is what the user experiences.

candidate_statements.statement: Where the software is waiting on processing or transmission and the wait exceeds a defined interval, the software shall inform the user, shall distinguish an absent connection from a transfer that is failing, and shall offer a route to support where the condition persists after retry.
candidate_statements.why: The longest wait in the flow is actively guarded in the shipping product: a fixed interval raises an alert, repetition escalates to retry or support, and a missing connection is named as such. The corpus describes only a passive waiting card, so a specification written from it alone would ship an unguarded indefinite wait with no exit.
candidate_statements.note: Sits between the flow and transmission areas; if the transmission requirements gain a stalled-transfer rule, fold this into it rather than keeping two.

requirements_needed.how_to_read: uncovered means no requirement in the revision named above describes this behaviour at all — it needs new wording. partly_covered means a requirement exists but does not describe what ACR actually does. Neither is a defect in ACR; both are decisions for Product.

prompt:
This JSON records how the current ACR application (Minuteful Kidney US) actually behaves today for E05 — Assay Timing Control. It covers F05.1 Timer framework and elapsed-time derivation, F05.2 Sample-freshness window, F05.3 Incubation gate and release-button window, F05.4 Colour-evolution gate and scanning window, F05.5 Timing display and expiry notification, F05.6 Timing invalidation messaging, F04.8 Waiting-time card.

It was read from the shipping source at iosDip develop @ e0636af31, AndroidDip develop @ a50d8b03e, android.shared-chat master @ 0d5db76db, android.shared-urine-algo master @ abe366b88, ios-chat-services master @ 4a4dbf440, ios-foundations master @ cf743d568, and checked against Rev 1.24 · Epic Map Rev 1.18. Every coverage verdict below is relative to that revision — a newer revision may already have closed a gap this file reports.

It is a record of existing behaviour. It is not a specification, and it is not a design to copy: ACR is a different product with a different kit, so its behaviour is evidence about a problem already solved once, not a decision about what QACR should do.
Product triaged every feature in this epic as new or changed, so this file is the DEPARTURE BASELINE — what QACR departs from. A `change` mark is the expected answer, not a defect in the reading; `correct` means QACR keeps this behaviour as-is.

How it is shaped:
- `features[].scenarios[].lines[]` — 181 behaviours, each one sentence. Each carries what iOS does, what Android does, and `platforms`, which is `same` where they agree and `differs` where they do not.
- Product's marks and comments are recorded per line: every behaviour carries its own `pm_mark` and `pm_comment` (`review_item` equals the line id).
- `coverage` on every line is stated, never implied: `covered`, `partly`, `uncovered`, or `not-mapped`. Do not read an empty `requirements` array as meaning nothing covers it — read `coverage`.

The three things that need a decision:
- **`requirements_needed.uncovered_behaviours`** (16) — ACR does these and no requirement describes them. `candidate_statements` proposes wording in the requirements document's own voice; adopt, reword or drop it as you see fit.
- **`requirements_needed.partly_covered_behaviours`** (119) — a requirement exists but does not describe what ACR actually does.
- **`not_knowable_from_code`** (39) — behaviour that cannot be established by reading source, because it is decided by the backend, sits inside a compiled component, or needs the app run to observe. **Do not specify any of these from this file.**
